Notably, none of the companies has been accused of wrongdoing, and prosecutors have not sought court-appointed administration for any of them. Instead, authorities are examining the companies’ supply-chain oversight as part of the broader investigation into alleged labor exploitation involving subcontractors . The latest development builds on a series of high-profile enforcement actions. Earlier this year, police in Milan arrested a Chinese national and shuttered a clandestine workshop on the city’s outskirts that produced clothing for unnamed fashion brands. The site was found to employ 10 Chinese workers, six of whom were unregistered and five of whom were living in Italy without legal status. According to authorities, the workers endured extreme conditions, laboring up to 90 hours per week for as little as €4 an hour while sleeping in makeshift, unhygienic dormitories inside the workshop. The investigation was triggered by a worker’s complaint after his hand was allegedly broken by an employer when he attempted to recover €10,000 in unpaid wages. It followed closely from a separate case involving Valentino. In May 2025, an Italian court placed Valentino Bags Lab under judicial administration after finding that it had subcontracted production to Chinese-owned firms that exploited workers. The court, however, lifted the measure early in April 2026 after Valentino strengthened its governance safeguards, introduced a more rigorous supplier qualification process, and enhanced its systems for monitoring and controlling its supply chain. The matter mirrored earlier judicial administration orders involving units of Armani and Dior after Milan prosecutors uncovered exploitative subcontracting networks in the production of luxury leather goods. Separately, Italy’s Competition Authority (“ AGCM “) closed its consumer protection investigation into a Dior-owned company after the brand agreed to a package of voluntary commitments stemming from judicial findings that exposed sweatshop-like conditions in subcontracted workshops producing luxury handbags. The investigation centered on whether Dior’s public representations regarding ethics, craftsmanship, and its supply chain could mislead consumers in light of the labor conditions uncovered within portions of its manufacturing network. Without establishing any infringement of consumer protection law, the AGCM accepted Dior’s commitments and closed the matter. Under the settlement, Dior agreed to strengthen its supplier selection and auditing procedures, enhance oversight throughout its supply chain, and contribute €2 million over five years to initiatives aimed at identifying and supporting victims of labor exploitation. “Dior remains committed to upholding our values of transparency and respect throughout our supply chain,” the company said in a statement. “We continue to closely monitor, and where appropriate, strengthen, our internal procedures to maintain fair and equitable working conditions for everyone who contributes, with great commitment and skill, to creating the finest quality Dior products.” What began with investigations into individual workshops and judicial administration orders involving certain luxury companies has evolved into broader scrutiny of the governance structures, supplier qualification procedures, auditing practices, and supply-chain controls luxury brands use to oversee their manufacturing networks. For luxury brands, the legal focus is no longer confined to the conditions uncovered inside a factory – it extends to the systems designed to prevent those conditions from arising in the first place. These developments are not isolated. Over the past several years Italian magistrates have exposed widespread abuse in the fashion and luxury sectors, prompting legal and administrative reforms aimed at closing the gap between luxury’s crafted image and the exploitative practices that often sustain it. A 2024 proposal from Milan’s court urges fashion companies to adopt stricter oversight procedures to ensure labor law compliance among suppliers. Italy is home to a dense network of small manufacturers – estimated to produce more than half of the world’s luxury goods , according to Bain & Company. While these workshops play a critical role in the industry’s global dominance, they also represent a vulnerability: a fragmented supply chain that allows major brands to outsource production with minimal visibility, creating fertile ground for labor abuses to flourish. Regulators are asking not only what happened inside supplier facilities but also whether luxury brands had adequate systems in place to detect and prevent labor abuses. And they are not just focusing on labor violations themselves but also on the systems luxury companies use to prevent them. Supplier qualification procedures, auditing practices, governance structures, and ongoing oversight have become central features of Italy’s enforcement strategy, reflecting a broader expectation that brands exercise meaningful control over increasingly complex supply chains. With authorities continuing to raid workshops, place luxury companies under judicial administration, resolve consumer protection investigations, and seek governance records from some of the industry’s biggest names, a clear pattern has emerged. Italy’s enforcement efforts have expanded beyond uncovering labor abuses themselves to scrutinizing whether luxury companies have implemented meaningful governance and oversight systems to prevent them. As the industry grapples with its social responsibilities, Italy’s message is clear: luxury cannot come at the cost of the law. Share

article_title: Gymshark Pulled into Growing Influencer Marketing Litigation Wave
sub_title: Gymshark is the latest brand to face a proposed class action lawsuit over its influencer marketing practices.
article_content: Gymshark is the latest brand to face a proposed class action over its influencer marketing practices, with a new lawsuit accusing the activewear company of systematically disguising paid influencer promotions as authentic endorsements in order to drive sales and command premium prices. In the June 16 complaint, plaintiff Mihaela Lupea alleges that Gymshark has “built a multi-billion-dollar apparel empire on misleading social media marketing strategies that systemically masquerade paid influencer promotion as authentic endorsements of [its] products.” Going beyond allegations that influencers simply failed to include “#ad” or similar disclosures in their social media posts, Lupea asserts in the complaint she filed with the Southern District of New York that undisclosed influencer marketing is a central component of Gymshark’s business strategy. I In particular, she alleges that Gymshark entered into “exclusive relationships “with influencers that prohibited them from “endorsing, advertising, or wearing competing brands.” The problem, per Lupea, is that the influencers failed to disclose both that they were “paid to endorse Gymshark’s products” and that Gymshark “prohibits them from endorsing other products.” And she maintains that Gymshark “intentionally, deceptively, and systemically causes paid social media influencers to post advertisements that appear to be non-sponsored, ‘organic’ content.” Against that background, Lupea asserts a claim under New York’s consumer protection law and alternative unjust-enrichment claims, and is seeking class certification, as well as damages and equitable relief. The complaint is the latest in a growing wave of proposed class actions in which plaintiffs are citing alleged influencer disclosure failures as the basis for state-law consumer protection claims. Since early 2025, consumer class actions have targeted influencer marketing efforts by Celsius, Shein, Revolve , ALO Yoga, and Beach Bunny, among others. The complaints – which target companies ranging from energy drink makers to swimwear brands – follow the same basic framework. They accuse companies and influencers of either omitting sponsorship disclosures altogether or presenting them in ways that are allegedly too obscure to be “clear and conspicuous,” causing consumers to mistake sponsored endorsements for independent recommendations. Unlike several of the earlier lawsuits, which named both brands and individual influencers as defendants, Lupea’s complaint targets Gymshark alone, focusing on Gymshark’s alleged responsibility for the challenged marketing practices. Because the Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) Act does not provide a private right of action, consumer plaintiffs have generally relied on state consumer protection and advertising laws, while pointing to the FTC’s Endorsement Guides as the benchmark for what adequate disclosures should have looked like. The alleged injury is also largely the same across the cases. The plaintiffs – who are seeking more than $500 million in some cases – contend that they either would not have purchased the products or would have paid less for them had they known the endorsements were sponsored. As such, the lawsuits rely on a familiar “price premium” theory, arguing that the appearance of authenticity increased demand and enabled brands to command higher prices. That theory does not depend on allegations that the products themselves were defective or failed to perform as advertised. Instead, plaintiffs contend that undisclosed sponsorships distorted consumers’ purchasing decisions and inflated the prices they paid. Whether those claims ultimately succeed, however, remains an open question. While some courts have found comparable allegations sufficient to establish standing at the pleading stage, others have required plaintiffs to tie the challenged marketing more concretely to the products’ value or the alleged overpayment. The cases have produced different procedural outcomes thus far. The ALO Yoga litigation was resolved through a settlement before the court reached the merits, while the Revolve court compelled the plaintiff’s claims to arbitration and struck the class allegations . The Shein and Beach Bunny cases remain pending. In the Celsius case, the court dismissed the claims against two influencer defendants without leave to amend and dismissed the remaining claims with leave to amend; the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint on July 8. THE BIGGER PICTURE : The growing number – and similarity – of these lawsuits suggests that alleged influencer disclosure failures are evolving beyond an FTC compliance issue. Depending on the statute invoked, these claims may open the door to statutory damages, restitution, and attorneys’ fees, making alleged disclosure failures potentially attractive vehicles for class litigation. For brands that rely heavily on creators to build awareness and drive sales, disclosure practices are becoming part of the broader consumer litigation risk landscape. The case is Lupea v. Gymshark USA, Inc., 1:26-cv-05073 (S.D.N.Y.). Share

article_title: Sustainability Funding and M&A Tracker
sub_title: Here is a running timeline of the most notable fashion and luxury-focused sustainability and ESG M&A and investments.
article_content: Sustainability is reshaping investment across fashion and retail, as brands, manufacturers, and investors direct capital toward technologies and business models aimed at reducing the industry’s environmental footprint and adapting to a growing body of climate- and sustainability-focused regulation . Investment is flowing into textile recycling and circularity, next-generation materials, lower-impact manufacturing, supply-chain traceability, resale and repair infrastructure, and technologies designed to help companies measure and manage their environmental impact, against a backdrop of mounting scrutiny over sustainability claims and greenwashing . Against that backdrop, this tracker follows notable funding rounds, mergers and acquisitions, strategic investments, and other transactions involving sustainability-focused companies and initiatives with a meaningful connection to fashion, beauty, retail, and consumer goods. The running timeline provides a view of where capital is flowing across the sector and how the technologies, materials, and business models underpinning the industry’s sustainability efforts are evolving. French recycling startup Syntetica has raised $30 million in Series A funding to scale its patented nylon recycling technology and build its first commercial demonstration facility in France. The round was led by Bpifrance’s Ecotechnologies 2 fund, with participation from lululemon, MAS Holdings, SWEN Capital Partners, EQT Ventures, and several strategic family offices. Syntetica’s technology can recycle both Nylon 6 and Nylon 6,6 from mixed post-consumer textile waste without requiring prior separation, addressing a major barrier to textile circularity. The funding will support industrial-scale deployment of the technology in partnership with Michelin’s Centre for Sustainable Materials. “For decades, mixed nylon waste has been considered too complex and too expensive to recycle at scale,” said co-founder and CEO Marco Bertone. “This funding allows us to move from breakthrough chemistry to industrial reality and accelerate the transition to more circular materials.” Berlin-based reverse.fashion has secured a seven-figure extension to its pre-seed funding round from High-Tech Gründerfonds (HTGF). Founded in 2024, the company develops AI-powered textile sorting technology that uses computer vision, machine learning, and Digital Product Passport integration to automate the classification of used garments for reuse, resale, repair, upcycling, or recycling. The funding will support the commercial rollout of its co.sort software and line.sort automated sorting system. According to the company, its technology can increase sorting productivity by 40% and boost recovered value by 20%, helping accelerate circularity across the fashion industry Fashion sustainability data platform Carbonfact has acquired Berlin-based Vaayu as brands face growing pressure to comply with product-level environmental disclosure regulations. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. The acquisition combines Carbonfact’s network of more than 200 fashion brands, including On, Ganni, and The North Face, with Vaayu’s expertise in retail climate data and product-level emissions tracking. The combined platform will serve more than 300 apparel and footwear brands globally. Founded in 2020 by former Zalando sustainability executive Namrata Sandhu, Vaayu developed one of fashion’s earliest product-level carbon accounting platforms and was backed by Atomico and CapitalT. Carbonfact is backed by Alven, Headline, and Y Combinator. The companies said the merger will help brands prepare for upcoming regulations including Digital Product Passports, France’s Eco-Score framework, and California’s SB253 climate disclosure rules. Carbonfact also said it is developing AI-powered “Environmental Intelligence” tools to help fashion companies manage emissions data and sustainability compliance workflows at scale. French textile upcycling startup Losanje has raised €6.7 million in funding to expand production capacity and accelerate the industrialization of its garment upcycling platform. The round included support from existing investors UI Investissement and Crédit Agricole, alongside new backers including Lita, Evolem, and Albo. Public institutions including ADEME, Bpifrance, and the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté Region also participated. Founded by Simon Peyronnaud and Mathieu Khouri, Losanje specializes in transforming unsold and used garments into new products for fashion brands through automated cutting and industrial upcycling processes. “This round marks a pivotal step in the emergence of an industrial upcycling sector,” said co-founder Simon Peyronnaud. The funding will support production expansion, new industrial equipment, R&D, and the relocation of operations to a larger 2,500-square-meter facility in Nevers as the company aims to position upcycling as a scalable pillar of the circular fashion economy. Fashion-tech company unspun has raised $32 million in an oversubscribed Series B funding round led by DCVC, with participation from Lowercarbon Capital, E12, Decathlon, and SOSV. The company plans to use the funding to expand deployment of its Vega™ 3D weaving technology across Europe and North America. Founded in the U.S., unspun develops automated weaving systems capable of producing garments directly from yarn within minutes, aiming to localize apparel manufacturing while reducing waste, inventory, and carbon emissions across fashion supply chains. The company partners with brands and manufacturers focused on decarbonization and supply chain efficiency through low-impact, on-demand production models. Bestseller has invested $3 million into the Regenerative Fund for Nature to support regenerative agriculture initiatives in South Africa’s Eastern Cape. The fund, launched by Conservation International and Kering, with Inditex joining in 2023, works with local communities to restore ecosystems and promote sustainable farming practices. Bestseller’s investment will support projects led by sheep farmers and shepherds focused on restoring grasslands, improving soil health, enhancing animal welfare, and reducing climate-related risks. The initiative aligns with Bestseller’s Fashion FWD sustainability strategy, which integrates biodiversity and ecosystem restoration into its supply chain and long-term raw material sourcing efforts. The Bezos Earth Fund has announced $34 million in new grants to accelerate the development of sustainable, next-generation materials for the fashion and textile industry. The funding supports research into innovative fibers designed to replicate the look and performance of traditional materials like cotton, silk, and rayon, while improving environmental impact through biodegradability, reduced land use, and lower emissions. “That’s not just good for the planet. That’s the future of fashion,” said Vice Chair Lauren Sánchez Bezos. Grant recipients include: Columbia University ($11.5M), developing bacteria-grown textile fibers from agricultural waste in partnership with the Fashion Institute of Technology; University of California, Berkeley ($10M), creating biodegradable fibers inspired by spider silk; Clemson University ($11M), engineering next-generation cotton using gene editing and synthetic biology; and The Cotton Foundation ($1.5M), restoring a global non-GMO cotton seedbank. The initiative underscores growing momentum behind bio-based and circular materials as the fashion industry looks to reduce its environmental footprint while maintaining performance and scalability. Reju has secured €135 million in funding from the Dutch government’s NIKI program to support the development of an industrial-scale textile-to-textile regeneration hub at Chemelot Industrial Park. The project will focus on recycling polyester-based textiles into new, high-quality materials, helping reduce reliance on virgin inputs and divert waste from landfill and incineration. The regenerated output, branded as Reju Polyester, is expected to deliver around 50% lower carbon emissions compared to traditional polyester. “This award is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and our team,” said CEO Patrik Frisk. The funding will support both construction and operations, positioning the Chemelot facility as a blueprint for scaling circular textile infrastructure across Europe. UK-based Epoch Biodesign has raised $12 million in funding, with participation from lululemon, Kompas VC, Happiness Capital, Extantia, and Leitmotif, bringing total funding to over $50 million. The company is focused on solving one of fashion’s toughest challenges: recycling nylon 6,6 at scale. Its proprietary enzyme-based process uses AI and synthetic biology to break down waste nylon into its original monomers, enabling the production of virgin-quality materials without fossil inputs. Unlike traditional methods, it can process complex materials like blended textiles and coated fabrics. The funding will support the move from pilot to large-scale demonstration, advancing commercial production and industry partnerships. Rubi has raised $7.5 million in funding co-led by AP Ventures and FH One Investments, with participation from investors including H&M Group, Talis Capital, and CMPC Ventures. The round follows strong commercial momentum, including over $60 million in offtake agreements with fashion brands and manufacturers. The company is developing a proprietary enzyme-based platform that converts CO₂ into essential materials, enabling the production of textiles and other inputs without relying on fossil resources. Its modular system is designed to support more flexible, lower-cost manufacturing across industries. “We’ve now demonstrated this technology scales effectively and meets or exceeds customer product standards,” said CEO Neeka Mashouf. The funding will support scaling to industrial production and expanding applications across textiles, consumer goods, and chemicals. India-based startup Canvaloop has raised $1.43 million in funding led by GVFL, with participation from Rockstud Capital. Founded in 2020, the company converts agricultural waste into spinnable textile materials, including hemp, flax, banana, nettle, and pine-based fibers compatible with existing manufacturing systems. The funding will be used to scale production capacity from 30 to 300 tonnes per month, expand the team, and advance R&D in regenerative cellulose materials. Swiss biomaterials company Seprify has raised €13.4 million (CHF12.25 million) in a Series A funding round to scale its cellulose-based materials platform. The round included investors Inter IKEA Group, Una Terra, Zürcher Kantonalbank (ZKB), Cambridge Enterprise Ventures, and Kickfund, alongside other circular-economy-focused backers. Seprify develops high-performance cellulose ingredients designed as sustainable alternatives to traditional materials. The funding will support commercial production, expand industrial partnerships, and accelerate the deployment of bio-based materials across multiple industries. Nonprofit organization Soles4Souls has acquired Erren Recondition, a Netherlands-based footwear and apparel reconditioning company. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Founded in Arnhem and operating for more than 130 years, Erren Recondition provides services including mold cleaning, repairs, finishing, labeling, and packaging. The company will continue operating in Europe under the name Erren Recondition, a Soles4Souls company. The acquisition expands Soles4Souls’ ability to help brands and retailers extend product life, reduce waste, and support circularity initiatives by refurbishing footwear and apparel for resale, reuse, or donation. Colorado-based outdoor apparel company Jack and Sage has acquired the assets, intellectual property, and inventory of sustainable apparel brand Kastlfel. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition expands Jack and Sage’s presence in premium logo wear across national parks, ski resorts, and outdoor destinations while adding a line of sustainable basics including tees, knitwear, and headwear. Kastlfel is known for using 100% sustainable materials such as organic cotton and recycled fibers. The deal also includes a partnership with Kastlfel’s parent company Ecocentric Brands to continue sustainability-focused screen printing operations in Denver. UK startup Shellworks has raised $15 million in Series A funding to scale production of Vivomer, its 100% compostable alternative to plastic used in beauty packaging.The round was led by Alter Equity, with participation from Nat Friedman, JamJar, and existing investors Founder Collective, LocalGlobe, and Third Sphere. Vivomer, a biopolymer created through microbial fermentation, can be used to produce rigid or flexible packaging and fully biodegrades within about a year. Beauty brands including Unilever’s Wild, Hair by Sam McKnight, Wildsmith, and Sonsie are already using the material. Advanced biotechnology company Ecovia Bio has closed a Series B funding round led by Pointe Angels to expand production capacity at its Livonia, Michigan facility. The capital will support a major scale-up of the company’s AzuraBase and AzuraGel product lines, gamma polyglutamic acid (γ-PGA) and specialty biopolymers used in cosmetics, personal care, agriculture, and hygiene applications. These biodegradable materials are designed to replace conventional petroleum-based superabsorbent polymers (SAPs), which contribute to long-term landfill waste and microplastic pollution. “This funding enables us to meet immediate customer demand while building the infrastructure required to serve the hygiene sector at industrial scale,” said CEO Kousay Said. Swiss traceability startup Haelixa has secured €2 million in a Pre-Series A funding round to accelerate global expansion and deepen partnerships with textile brands. The round was led by Verve Ventures and Zurich Kantonalbank, with participation from 212 NexT Fund. Haelixa’s proprietary technology uses DNA markers to tag and trace raw materials and products throughout the supply chain, offering brands proof of origin and production transparency. The company aims to scale internationally and position its solution as a critical tool for supply chain integrity amid rising regulatory and consumer pressure. The investment supports Haelixa’s long-term strategy to work closely with brands across fashion and textiles seeking robust, science-based traceability. Sparxell, a University of Cambridge spinout developing bioinspired, plastic-free colourants, has raised €4.2 million ($5 million) in pre-Series A funding to commercialize its cellulose-based pigment technology. The round was led by SWEN Capital Partners’ Blue Ocean 2 fund, with support from Alpha Star Capital and Cambridge Enterprise. Founded by Dr. Benjamin Droguet and Professor Silvia Vignolini, Sparxell creates vibrant colours using natural cellulose crystals, mimicking the iridescence seen in butterfly wings. Its patented structural colour platform enables the production of biodegradable pigments, inks, glitters, sequins, and films without toxic chemicals or plastics. “This funding takes us from proof of concept to production and commercial launches,” said CEO Droguet. Tonne-scale manufacturing is expected by the end of 2026. Lenzing Group has acquired a controlling majority stake in Swedish innovation company TreeToTextile AB, strengthening its position in sustainable, wood-based specialty fibers. The transaction, completed through the issuance of new shares, deepens Lenzing’s investment in a patent-protected, highly scalable cellulosic fiber technology. H&M Group, Inter IKEA Group, Stora Enso, and LSCS Invest will remain minority shareholders, continuing to support the platform with market, consumer, and long-term strategic expertise. TreeToTextile’s process is positioned as a major technological advance in fiber production, offering improved sustainability, cost efficiency, and broad applicability across textile and nonwoven markets. With majority ownership, Lenzing will accelerate the development of a demonstration plant and prepare for a large-scale industrial facility. “TreeToTextile is among the world’s most advanced next-generation fiber technologies,” said Georg Kasperkovitz, COO of Lenzing Group. “We are fully committed to the joint scale-up and commercialization.” Retail circularity platform SuperCircle has raised $24 million in Series A funding to expand its AI-driven infrastructure for managing and monetizing textile waste. The round was led by Foundry with participation from BBG Ventures, Renewal Fund, and Elemental Impact. Headquartered in New York, SuperCircle partners with over 75 retailers, including J.Crew, GUESS, Reformation, FIGS, and Parachute Home, to power consumer trade-in programs and reverse logistics. Its technology analyzes item-level data to route goods through over 50 reuse and recycling streams, helping brands reduce write-downs, comply with regulatory shifts, and unlock new revenue from excess inventory. “With SuperCircle, we’re turning end-of-life into a value-generating phase of the product lifecycle,” said CEO and co-founder Chloe Songer. The funding will fuel product development, logistics expansion, and broader enterprise adoption as the company targets 1 billion diverted textiles by 2030. The Repsol Foundation has acquired a 14% stake in Coleo Network, the recycling division of Spanish textile circularity leader Coleo. The investment supports Coleo’s expansion plans across Europe, including the development of new industrial-scale waste management and recovery plants, and aligns with Repsol Foundation’s strategy of backing triple-impact projects focused on social inclusion, environmental protection and sustainable growth. Founded by CEO David Puyuelo, Coleo operates at the forefront of Europe’s textile recycling push. With more than 7 million tonnes of textile waste generated annually in the region – much of it still ending up in landfills or incineration – the company aims to industrialise circular solutions and reduce waste dependency. “This investment reflects our commitment to the triple-impact economy and advancing sustainability in strategic sectors like textile recycling,” said Repsol chairman Antonio Brufau. Brussels-based Resortecs has raised €6 million in Series A funding to accelerate the rollout of its Smart Stitch and Smart Disassembly technology across Europe. The funding will support the completion of the company’s first continuous industrial disassembly line and the deployment of five lines in total over the next five years. Resortecs’ patented thermal disassembly system is designed to streamline textile-to-textile recycling by enabling garments to be taken apart at scale without manual intervention. The company plans to increase its processing capacity tenfold to 3,000 metric tonnes per year by 2027, helping brands and manufacturers meet circularity goals and divert waste from landfill. Dutch biotech startup Qorium has secured €22 million in Series A funding to scale its cell-grown leather production, marking a pivotal step from R&D to commercial manufacturing. The round was led by Invest-NL and LIOF, with continued support from Brightlands Venture Partners and Sofinnova Partners, and backed by the European Commission’s InvestEU guarantee scheme. Qorium creates real leather from a few animal cells – eliminating the need for livestock farming while dramatically reducing waste, water use, and emissions. The new capital will fund the installation of bioreactor systems at its Maastricht facility and accelerate its go-to-market strategy. With €30 million raised to date, Qorium is positioning itself as a global leader in sustainable materials innovation, targeting one of the most polluting industries in the world with a scalable, science-backed solution. “We’re creating real leather that outperforms the traditional version – without the environmental or ethical cost,” said CEO Michael Newton. Global holding company Inside Out LLC has acquired sustainable clothing brand The Simple Folk, marking a key step in its mission to reshape business through purpose-driven growth. Known for its minimalist, environmentally conscious designs, The Simple Folk will now operate under new CEO Luis Gamardo and gain access to Inside Out’s global infrastructure and sustainability expertise. The brand will collaborate with WRAD, Inside Out’s impact consulting studio, to align future expansion with the group’s ‘Towards a Thriving Future’ framework—focusing on environmental health, social responsibility, and long-term systemic change “Clothing is more than fabric, it’s a reflection of principle and care,” said Gamardo. “Inside Out gives us the platform to scale that belief globally, without compromise.” With the acquisition, Inside Out continues its commitment to backing companies that prioritize trust, wellbeing, and environmental stewardship alongside profit. Cambridge-based biomaterials startup PACT has raised £16 million in a Series A round led by Forbion and HV Capital to scale production of Oval , its patented collagen-based alternative to plastic-derived leathers like PVC. The funding will support the launch of a 20-meter pilot production line and drive commercial roll-to-roll manufacturing from PACT’s Cambridge HQ. Founded in 2020 by organic chemist Dr Yudí Ding and physicist-engineer Niels Ramay, PACT aims to replace synthetic leathers with Oval, a luxurious, durable, and designer-friendly material made from natural cosmetic-grade collagen infused with herbal oils and extracts. Compared to conventional faux leather, Oval uses less water and slashes CO₂ emissions while maintaining high aesthetic and tactile standards. The science is only the first step, the real challenge is scaling beautifully and sustainably,” said CEO Dr Yudí Ding. “With Oval, we’re delivering both innovation and impact.” London-based startup SAGES has secured £190,000 in funding from the British Design Fund to accelerate commercialization of its biodegradable, food-waste-derived dyes, an eco-friendly alternative to synthetic dyes, which contribute an estimated 20% of global wastewater. Founded by Emily Taylor and Alice Simpson, SAGES is pioneering water-soluble, non-toxic dyes sourced from waste streams like onion skins, coffee grounds, blueberries, and avocado. The startup’s patented formulations meet industry standards for UV and wash fastness and work with existing dyeing infrastructure. Recent collaborations include Patrick McDowell’s London Fashion Week collection, trials with Bananatex and Story Mfg, and surface projects with James Burleigh. The new capital will support pilot-scale production, product development, and partnerships across fashion, interiors, and industrial textiles. “We’re working to replace petroleum-based colourants with scalable, biodegradable alternatives that align with both industry needs and environmental urgency,” said co-founder Emily Taylor. Vienna-based refurbed, a leading marketplace for professionally refurbished electronics, sportswear, and ghomeoods, has raised £44 million in a funding round led by Alex Zubillaga and Orilla, with follow-on participation from existing investors including Evli Growth Partners, Bonsai, Almaz, C4 Ventures, and Speedinvest. Founded in 2017, refurbed promotes sustainable consumption by extending product lifecycles through refurbishment. The platform has processed 9 million devices, served 4 million customers across 12 European markets, and claims to have prevented 350,000 tons of CO₂ emissions and 1,136 tons of e-waste. The new capital will fuel growth in the UK, a key focus market for refurbed’s next phase of European expansion. “We’re rethinking consumption and helping people choose sustainability without compromising on quality,” said co-founder Peter Windischhofer. Indian materials science startup AltMat has announced new funding from a global investor group including H&M Group, Fashion for Good, Rainmatter by Zerodha, and Turbostart, as it scales its sustainable fiber innovation, Altag. Made entirely from agricultural residue like leftover food crop stems, Altag is positioned as a high-performance, low-impact alternative to conventional fibers. The fresh investment will support AltMat’s next phase of growth: expanding grassroots sourcing from Indian farmers, strengthening R&D, and accelerating international market entry. “Investing in AltMat is not just about backing material innovation, but about enabling a shift in the way our industry sources at scale,” said Laura Coppen, Investment Manager at H&M Group’s New Growth & Ventures. Finnish sustainable materials company Spinnova has acquired full ownership of Woodspin and Suzano Finland from joint venture partner Suzano S.A. The deal grants Spinnova exclusive rights to wood-based Spinnova fibre production, along with key assets including refining equipment, MFC technology, and 18 Suzano Finland employees who will now join the company. The joint venture will be dissolved as part of the agreement. London-based startup ZERØTEC has secured £642,000 in pre-seed funding to combat fashion’s staggering $300 billion annual fabric waste problem. The round was led by Bethnal Green Ventures, with backing from SFC Capital, SCE Freiraum Ventures, Cranfield University Seed Fund, and angel investor Benjamin Manwaring. Founded by former sustainability consultant Nicholas Betts, ZERØTEC uses AI-driven pattern optimisation to cut material waste at the design stage, offering up to 15% material savings for brands. The technology aims to eliminate waste before production begins, a sharp contrast to downstream recycling solutions. “We’re on a mission to solve one of fashion’s most critical problems with patented AI solutions that deliver real material benefits,” said Betts. “Our platform helps brands embrace sustainability, cut costs, and finally bring transparency to the true impact of our clothes.” With more than 250 brands already piloting its platform—including Fortune 500 apparel giants, ZERØTEC is gaining momentum as a category-defining solution in sustainable fashion tech. French startup EverDye has secured €15 million ($18 million) in fresh funding to scale its low-emission textile dyeing technology. The round was co-led by Crédit Mutuel Innovation and Daphni, as the fashion industry faces mounting pressure to reduce its environmental footprint. Founded in 2021 and based near Paris, EverDye claims its patented process uses lower temperatures, less water, and works with existing dyeing machinery, helping manufacturers cut both carbon emissions and operational costs. “Our solution not only promotes sustainability but also significantly reduces operational costs for manufacturers,” said Philippe Berlan, CEO of EverDye. “In an era where energy costs are a critical survival factor, EverDye’s innovation is a game-changer.” Textile recycling startup Refiberd has landed fresh investment and strategic support from PDS Ventures, extending its recent momentum following a major innovation award win in June. The Cupertino-based company, known for its plug-and-play AI technology that identifies garment material composition, will use the backing to expand integration into global sorting and recycling operations. Refiberd’s AI addresses a longstanding bottleneck in textile recycling, accurately sorting fabrics by fiber content, and aims to work within existing infrastructure rather than build standalone facilities. “The real unlock for us with PDS is that they can play both sides, moving conversations forward with customers, and also backing us financially,” said Sarika Bajaj, co-founder and CEO. “That’s the difference between surviving versus not, especially as market conditions get more strained.” French biotech company Carbios has confirmed €72 million in funding to begin construction of its first industrial textile recycling facility in Longlaville, Lorraine. The financing includes €42.5 million in support from ADEME and regional authorities, enabling the company to move forward with a project previously delayed. The plant will scale Carbios’ patented enzymatic depolymerization technology for PET, aiming to recycle the equivalent of 300 million synthetic T-shirts or two billion colored plastic bottles into virgin-quality material annually. “The recent regulatory boost and strong customer interest give us the confidence to move forward decisively,” said Managing Director Vincent Kamel. “This is a major step toward industrializing a circular economy for plastics and textiles.” YiLab, the materials science company co-founded by Stanford nanotech pioneer Yi Cui, has closed an oversubscribed pre-A funding round, bringing its total funding to over $10 million. The investment will accelerate the global rollout of its textile innovation platform LifeLabs Design, which creates sustainable, temperature-regulating fabrics for apparel and accessories. Built on a decade of Stanford research, LifeLabs fabrics reduce energy use by helping wearers stay cool or warm without relying on HVAC systems. The new funding will support the launch of a state-of-the-art R&D and manufacturing facility in Asia to speed prototyping and scale production. “This funding marks a pivotal step in our mission to transform textiles into powerful climate solutions,” said YiLab CEO and Co-Founder Sophia Ou. Materials science startup Everbloom has raised over $8 million in funding to advance its proprietary biodegradable fibers made from upcycled protein-rich waste. The round was led by Hoxton Ventures, with participation from SOSV, Tuesday Capital, Clocktower Ventures, and Brussels-based Endgame Capital. Everbloom’s next-gen textile technology addresses a critical sustainability gap in fashion by transforming waste into high-performance, planet-friendly materials. The funding will support the company’s next growth phase, including upcoming collaborations with premium fashion partners. “Everbloom is pioneering a category-defining platform for sustainable textiles,” said Hoxton Ventures’ Hussein Kanji. “Their breakthrough innovation has the potential to reshape how the fashion industry sources materials, and we’re excited to help them scale globally.” UK-based next-gen recycled leather fiber innovator Gen Phoenix has raised $15 million in a funding round led by Material Impact, with a significant follow-on investment from Tapestry, Inc., owner of Coach, Kate Spade, and Stuart Weitzman. Tapestry increased its equity stake to 9.9%, nearly quadrupling its 2023 position, and signed a three-year supply agreement as part of the deal. The new funding will support global expansion, increased production capacity at Gen Phoenix’s UK facility, and the commercialization of its fully circular leather solution. The move strengthens Tapestry’s future-ready supply chain while reinforcing its leadership in sustainable innovation. “This investment reflects our belief in the power of innovation to drive both purpose and profit. Gen Phoenix’s platform enables circularity at scale—delivering high-quality materials that meet the style, performance, and impact expectations of today’s consumer,” said Scott Roe, Tapestry Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer. Paris-based biotech Faircraft has acquired key assets from California startup VitroLabs in a strategic move to accelerate the industrialization of in vitro leather. The deal gives Faircraft access to VitroLabs’ high-end cultured leather demonstrations and a portfolio of 30 international patents covering innovations in tissue engineering, including multi-layered skin cultivation and scalable cell growth. Faircraft, which merges biotech and materials science to create sustainable alternatives for fashion and leather goods, now positions itself as a leader in the emerging lab-grown leather sector. “This marks a strategic turning point,” said CEO and Co-Founder Haïkel Balti. “Our goal is to make in vitro leather a mark of prestige for the world’s top fashion houses.” London-based biotech startup Solena Materials has raised $6.7 million in Seed funding to scale production of its AI-designed synthetic protein fibres—positioned as a sustainable, high-performance alternative to traditional textiles. The round was led by Sir David Harding, with continued backing from SynBioVen and Insempra, bringing Solena’s total funding to $10.8 million. Spun out of Imperial College London in 2022, Solena engineers fibres at the molecular level using AI and microbial fermentation to fine-tune properties like strength, flexibility, and texture. “We’re creating protein sequences that don’t exist in nature to meet modern performance and manufacturing needs,” said CEO and Co-Founder Dr. James MacDonald. The new capital will fund a facility expansion near Imperial and support new fashion industry partnerships. London-based Arda Biomaterials has raised $5.25 million in seed funding to scale production of its sustainable, leather-like materials made from spent barley sourced from beer and whisky makers. The round was led by Oyster Bay Venture Capital, with participation from Clean Growth Fund, Kadmos Capital, and Green Angel Ventures. The funding will support the buildout of a new facility five times larger than its current space, enabling Arda to scale its first product, New Grain, a plastic- and animal-free textile for fashion and automotive use. Based in London’s Bermondsey Beer Mile, Arda has already partnered with BEEN London on a snakeskin-style handbag made with locally sourced grain waste. “We’re connecting brewers and distillers with the fashion and automotive worlds,” said cofounder and CEO Brett Cotten. “That’s where real scale and impact happen.” German startup eeden has raised €18 million in a Series A round to accelerate its chemical textile recycling technology. The round was led by Forbion’s BioEconomy Fund, with backing from Henkel Ventures, NRW.Venture, and returning investors TechVision Fonds, High-Tech Gründerfonds, and D11Z Ventures. Based in Münster, eeden has developed a proprietary chemical process that upcycles cotton-polyester blends by recovering cellulose and breaking down polyester into reusable building blocks. These can be converted into high-quality fibers like lyocell, viscose, and polyester—providing a circular alternative to conventional textiles. The funding will support construction of eeden’s demonstration plant in Münster, scale industrial processing, and advance commercial partnerships across the textile industry. “eeden has developed a pioneering solution that can make large-scale textile recycling not only technologically feasible but also commercially viable,” said Forbion’s Alex Hoffmann. London-based climatetech startup 51toCarbonZero has raised £3 million in a new funding round led by Fuel Ventures, with support from angel investors. The investment will fuel the company’s expansion into Europe and the U.S., and advance its AI-powered platform designed to help corporations manage and reduce their carbon emissions. 51toCarbonZero, whose clients include ETRO, Wolf, Sonobi, and KNESKO Skin, offers a solution that meets rising demands for emissions transparency and regulatory compliance. “We’ve built a platform that empowers businesses to make real progress toward net zero,” said the team. Fuel Ventures, a returning investor, reaffirmed its confidence in the company’s mission and rapid growth. Trove has acquired Reverse.supply, a Berlin-based resale marketplace, as part of its strategy to expand internationally and strengthen its technology offering for brands implementing circular solutions. The deal, the terms of which have not been disclosed, follows Trove’s acquisition of Recurate in August 2024 and positions the resale technology company to better serve growing demand across Europe, the UK, and North America. “The timing of this transaction is pivotal, as brands and retailers in Europe are facing new legislation and actively seeking profitable, future-proof revenue streams,” said Janis Künkler, Co-Founder of Reverse.supply. “By bringing Trove’s proven technology to Europe, we’re positioned to help brands navigate these changes and build successful resale programmes.” Simplifyber, a startup developing bio-based alternatives to traditional textiles, has raised $12 million (€10.5 million) in a funding round led by Suzano Ventures. The company’s proprietary material, Fybron, is both biodegradable and designed for 3D injection molding—eliminating the need for spinning, weaving, cutting, or sewing in the production of soft goods. The funding will support scientific development, mechanical engineering, and expanded production, as well as new facilities and strategic partnerships. Simplifyber recently partnered with Danish fashion brand Ganni to produce a shoe upper made entirely from its material, marking an early step toward commercial adoption. Paris-based Fairly Made, a scale-up driving sustainability in fashion, has raised €15 million in funding to accelerate its evolution into a pure technology player. The round was led by BNP Paribas Solar Impulse Venture Fund, along with GET Fund, ETF Partners, and Frenchfounders. “This funding allows us to scale our SaaS platform, expand our expert team, and support global growth,” said co-founder Laure Betsch. Fairly Made’s 360° platform enables fashion brands to track supply chains, assess environmental impact, and increase consumer transparency. The company currently supports clients including LVMH, Versace, A.P.C., and Paul Smith. Sheep Inc has raised £5 million ($6.48 million) in a Series A funding round led by Inside Out LLC. The London-based fashion brand, known for its industry-first carbon-negative supply chain and regenerative Merino wool garments, will use the funds to scale its operations, expand its Connected Dot technology, and accelerate its mission to set new standards for sustainability and transparency in fashion. “Sheep Inc stands at the forefront of responsible fashion,” said Suzy Amis Cameron, founder of Inside Out. “With its pioneering carbon-negative production, regenerative Merino wool, and innovative Connected Dot technology, it’s setting a new benchmark for transparency and quality.” Lululemon has signed a multi-year agreement with biotech company ZymoChem to scale its use of bio-based nylon, expanding on a partnership that began with a $21 million Series A investment last year. The athleticwear brand is making a minority investment to help commercialize ZymoChem’s technology for producing adipic acid, a traditionally petroleum-based ingredient critical to nylon 6,6. According to Lululemon, the resulting bio-nylon offers the same performance and feel as conventional materials and is already featured in popular styles like its Align and Wunder Train leggings, supporting the brand’s shift toward more sustainable raw materials. “We spent years refining our patented Carbon Conserving process with a vision to develop a sustainable version of nylon,” said Harshal Chokhawala, Co-Founder & CEO of ZymoChem. “We are thrilled to have deepened our engagement with lululemon, setting the stage for our technologies to deliver bio-based and decarbonized nylon on a global scale.” Textile-to-textile recycling pioneer Circ has raised $25 million in funding, led by investment firm Taranis through its Carbon Ventures fund. This latest round will support Circ’s transition from demonstration-scale to industrial-scale production, accelerating its mission to revolutionize textile circularity. Existing investors Avery Dennison and Inditex, which previously collaborated with Circ on a 2023 Zara collection featuring recycled polycotton textiles, also participated in the round. With the new capital, Circ is now plotting its first industrial-scale textile recycling plant, furthering its ability to separate and recover blended polyester-cotton fibers, a major challenge in textile waste management. Circ CEO Peter Majeranowski emphasized that this phase demands world-class engineering, operations, and investment from aligned partners, noting that Taranis’ industrial expertise will be instrumental in scaling the company’s impact. This investment builds on Circ’s prior $25 million funding in 2023 and $30 million Series B round in 2022, solidifying its position as a leader in circular fashion technology. Despite challenges in textile recycling financing, Taranis CEO Emmanuel Colombel sees Circ as a breakthrough solution for sustainability in fashion, reinforcing their commitment to reducing waste and emissions at scale. Epoch Biodesign has raised $18.3 million in a funding round led by Extantia Capital, with participation from Lowercarbon Capital, Inditex, and others. The London-based biotech startup will use the funds to scale its AI-driven plastic biorecycling technology, expand its enzyme library, and build its first commercial-scale recycling plant in the UK, set to launch in 2025. Epoch’s proprietary enzymatic process accelerates plastic degradation, with a focus on Nylon 6 recycling for the textile industry. The company plans to double its team size over the next year and aims to make recycled plastic cheaper than virgin materials, paving the way for large-scale adoption by major fashion brands. Jacob Nathan, founder and CEO of Epoch Biodesign, emphasized the company’s vision, stating, “We are building our first biorecycling plant to serve some of the most important clients in the textile industry. This funding allows us to expand our enzyme library to tackle materials that were previously non-recyclable.” H&M Foundation has committed $15.4 million to the Fashion ReModel project, which aims to showcase commercial alternatives to traditional garment production through rental, repair, resale, and remake models. The non-profit arm of the Swedish fashion giant will support the project over the next three years to scale circular business models and help decouple revenue from production. The initiative, first unveiled at the 2024 Global Fashion Summit in Copenhagen, brings together leading brands to find solutions, overcome challenges, and promote circular economy practices. Participating companies will commit to growing their revenue share from circular models and will report progress annually to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. Christiane Dolva, Head of Innovation, Research, and Demonstration at H&M Foundation, stated, “Embracing circular business models is essential—there’s simply no credible path to meeting global climate and biodiversity targets without transforming the way we do business.” GreenStitch has raised $1.2 million in a Seed round led by Equirus InnovateX Fund, with participation from Ivycap Ventures, Warmup Ventures, and Zeca Ventures. The round also saw participation from climate and fashion experts and entrepreneurs, such as Anshuman Bapna (founder, Terra.do), Sumit Jain (CTO, Zalora), Pankaj Vermani (founder, Clovia), Amit kumar (founder, Nobroker), and Senthil Sankar (founder, Ecoline). The Bengaluru-based  sustainability-focused SaaS platform designed for the fashion and textile industry will use the new funds to “strengthen its team and product and build a database for fashion and textiles.” Faircraft has raised $15.8 million in a new fundraising round backed by internationally-renowned investment funds, including Kindred Ventures (USA), Cap Horn (France), BPI (France), Sake Bosch (Netherlands), Entrepreneur First (UK), Alliance for Impact (France), and Heirloom (USA). The Paris-based “pioneer of lab-grown leather using unique and patented tissue engineering techniques” will sue the new funds to “expand its team, notably by recruiting more engineers and biologists, and accelerate its efforts to scale operations and meet growing demand.” “Lab-grown leather represents a major evolution that goes far beyond the fashion industry, and uses cutting-edge technologies to honour ethical considerations,” said Haïkel Balti, co-founder and CEO of Faircraft. “It enables the creation of unique pieces with minimal environmental impact, while offering new possibilities to leather artisans and designers. This technological breakthrough is a tribute to the magic of life.” Cold raised $2.65 million in a Pre-Seed funding round led by York IE, with participation from Better Ventures and a group of retail industry leaders. The Minneapolis, MN-based provider of a sustainability management platform says that it “leverages AI to streamline compliance for organizations of all sizes.” The company, whose clients include Bombas, Topo Designs, Outdoor Research, Fair Harbor, and Peak Design, will use the new funds to expand its engineering team and accelerate the development of new product features. “Sustainability reporting takes precious time and resources away from the important work of reducing an organization’s environmental impact,” said Eric Dayton, founder and CEO at Cold. “Cold solves this problem by centralizing and automating compliance so that sustainability leaders can focus on the work that matters most.” eBay will expand its Circular Fashion Fund, committing to providing a global investment of $1.2 million to start-ups in the global markets by the end of 2025. Designed to help fashion start-ups scale circular solutions, from production to end-of-life, including rental and repair services, the Circular Fashion Fund “is a catalyst for collaboration by combining the global scale and power of established companies like eBay with the creativity and innovation of nimble start-ups,” according to Kirsty Keoghan, Global GM of Fashion at eBay. “We’re not only helping to scale circular solutions but bringing together the most knowledgeable and respected experts in the industry. Together, we’re making a positive impact on the circular economy and truly reshaping the future of fashion.” Forward earth has raised €4.5 million in a Seed round led by Mosaic Ventures with participation from Speedinvest and European impact fund VC Revent. The Berlin-based startup, which touts itself as a leader in AI-powered environmental management solutions, will use the new funds to scale operations, expand to the U.S., and prepare for a future market launch in Asia. “By embedding environmental management into the existing business software of hundreds of thousands of companies,” forward earth says that it “simplifies the process of data collection, reporting, and regulatory compliance, particularly for businesses facing pressure from new regulations in the EU, U.K., and U.S.” Atlas Metrics has raised €12.2 million in a Series A round led by MMC Ventures with participation from existing investors Cherry Ventures, b2venture and Redstone. Te Berlin, Germany-based startup, which provides a platform for ESG compliance and sustainability performance management, will use the new funds to invest in its team, expand into new markets, and further develop its ESG compliance and performance management platform. Wladimir Nikoluk, Founder and CEO of Atlas Metrics, stated, “For all businesses across all industries, ESG reporting and compliance has become a necessary part of operations. But it is costly and risky to manage. This funding will allow us to enhance our product offerings, simplifying ESG compliance and turning sustainability data into a competitive advantage.” Briink has raised €3.85 million in a Seed round co-led by EquityPitcher Ventures and 13books Capital, with participation from existing investors Merantix, seed + speed Ventures, and notable angel investors. The Berlin-based startup, which is dedicated to empowering ESG and sustainability teams, will use the new funds to launch “a new AI product to help sustainability professionals extract actionable insights from environmental datasets, while building consistent and verifiable audit trails.” The company touts itself as offering “the world’s first AI agents designed specifically for ESG teams, accelerating their workflows while ensuring the highest level of data accuracy and quality.” “ESG professionals face a critical challenge: auditing and verifying vast amounts of data in a landscape still plagued by opacity and greenwashing,” said Tomas van der Heijden, co-founder and CEO of Briink. “High-quality, audited ESG data is essential to the climate transition, but manual processes and fragmented standards often compromise accuracy. Notpla has raised £20 million in a Series A round led by UB Forest Industry Green Growth Fund with participation from Catalytic Capital for Climate & Health (C3H), as well as Horizons Ventures and Astanor, including the Schmidt Family Foundation, Radicle Impact, EIT Food’s AgriFoodInvest, Broadwater Cap, Kibo Invest, Rosebrook, Trousdale Ventures, and Ocean Born Foundation. The London-based start up, which is developing sustainable seaweed-based packaging, counts Compass Group, Just Eat Takeaway.com, and sportswear brand Decathlon as customers. “We are thrilled to have secured this level of investment in such a competitive environment,” said Rodrigo Garcia Gonzalez, co-founder and co-CEO of Notpla. “This round not only validates our approach but also positions us to capitalize on the growing demand for truly plastic-free packaging solutions in global markets, especially as we look towards expansion into the U.S.” Datamaran Ltd. has raised $33 million in Series C financing from investment funds managed by Morgan Stanley. The London-headquartered software company that specializes in ESG offers an analytics platform for clients (including Dell Technologies Inc. and PepsiCo Inc.) to monitor risk and track adherence to the growing number of environmental, social, and governance-related regulations. Datamaran will use the new funds to accelerate its expansion in the U.S. and Europe, while driving innovation in generative AI technology. “This investment will enable us to stay at the forefront of innovation in AI-powered software to serve our clients’ growing needs,” said Marjella Lecourt-Alma, Datamaran’s co-founder and chief executive officer. Zevero has raised $7 million in a Seed funding round led by Spiral Capital, with participation from East Ventures and several angel investors. The Singapore-based global carbon accounting platform will sue the new funds to accelerate its scaling efforts in global key markets such as Japan, U.S., Australia, and Asia-Pacific countries. It will also will enable the company to “meet the increasing global demand for comprehensive sustainability solutions, with a particular focus on enhancing its decarbonization capabilities.” Shigeo Taniuchi co-founded and led Zevero says that it “helps supply-chain-heavy organizations meet sustainability goals by using AI to match emission factors, integrating supply chain data, and offering global climate expertise along their decarbonization journey. Amid rising regulatory and consumer demands, Zevero’s platform empowers businesses to assess their environmental impact across the full lifecycle of their products and operations.” Retraced has raised €15 million in a Series A funding round led by Partech, with participation from previous investors Alante Capital, Alstin Capital, Samaipata, and F-Log Ventures. The Germany-based online platform enables apparel brands to digitize, trace, and analyze sustainability compliance and risks in their supply chains in furtherance of its goal to “make sustainability management more effective and accessible for companies in the fashion and textile industry worldwide.” Lukas Pünder, CEO and co-Founder of Retraced, said, “This funding round marks a pivotal moment for Retraced. As the regulatory landscape becomes more complex, our mission to simplify sustainability management and make it more effective is more important than ever. With the support of our investors, we are well-positioned to continue developing our platform, empowering fashion brands to meet their sustainability goals and build stronger relationships with their suppliers and their customers.” GALY CO. has raised $33 million Series B financing led by Breakthrough Energy Ventures with additional participation from H&M Group and Zara-owner Inditex (as previously reported by TFL). The Boston-based climate tech company, which is “pioneering the development of first-of-its-kind sustainable cellular agriculture products,” will use the new funds to fuel the expansion of its research and development on its innovative cellular agriculture platform and “GALY Cotton.” Its “flagship” cotton product uses “99 percent less water and 97 percent less land than traditional cotton while emitting 77 percent less CO2, as it advances towards pre-industrial quality and scale,” the company says. Luciano Bueno, CEO and Founder of GALY said, “We are thrilled to have investors who recognize the crucial role that our climate adaptation technology will play in our daily lives. Climate change exposes the fragility of agricultural supply chains, and the recent rise in cocoa prices is a stark reminder of the new normal we face. Unfortunately, it’s not a matter of ‘if,’ but ‘when.’ Soon, the world will face increased volatility in conventional agriculture as extreme weather conditions become more frequent. When that time comes, GALY will be ready, better equipping our economy to withstand these shocks.” Tingit has raised €500,000 in a Pre-Seed round led by Firstpick, a Lithuanian VC fund, and accelerator for tech startups in the Baltics, with participation from BADideas.fund (Latvia), PurposeTech (Czech Republic), and Heartfelt Capital (Germany). The Lithuanian repairs marketplace aims to enable consumers to repair apparel items by connecting consumers with repair specialist via its app, which offers a repair experience with service booking, payment and shipping fully integrated into the platform. Tingit plans to use the new funds to launch the Service Provider Gateway, which “will enable any repair specialist to independently offer their services through the platform.” After a successful start in Lithuania, the startup plans to expand to other countries as well as introduce additional industries such as sports goods, toys, and consumer electronics. Under Armour, Inc. has acquired UNLESS COLLECTIVE, INC. in a deal that was finalized this week. The terms of the acquisition have not been disclosed. Co-founded in 2020 by adidas veteran Eric Liedtke, who will join Under Armour as its Executive Vice President of Brand Strategy, Unless Collective touts itself as “the world’s first all-plant, zero-plastic regenerative fashion brand.” Under Armour said in a statement that Liedtke will be “globally accountable for amplifying Under Armour’s brand identity and storytelling, its comprehensive strategic planning process, and executing transformational initiatives that accelerate growth for UA while continuing to lead and curate, UNLESS.” The sportswear company further stated that UNLESS, which “creates clothing and apparel built from the elements that can be worn in the elements and safely returned to the elements, is a collective of innovators, engineers, artists, and activists collaborating to operate the first regenerative fashion platform – connecting material, design, manufacturing, and composting to use plant-based innovation and production ingenuity to solve for a plastic-free future.” Inditex has taken a stake in Galy, the Boston-based sustainable agriculture startup. While the terms of the deal have not been disclosed, Inditex CEO Oscar Garcia Maceiras said that it comes in furtherance of the Spanish retail giant’s “broader strategy to support the sustainable economy,” noting that Galy’s development of “an innovative process to produce cotton in laboratories from plant cells … is a groundbreaking method [that] aims to revolutionize cotton production, potentially reduce environmental impact.” Sweden-based investment firm Altor has acquired the assets of Renewcell, the Swedish cotton textiles recycling company that filed for bankruptcy in February 2024 . The terms of the deal have not been disclosed. “This acquisition marks a new chapter for Renewcell, now renamed Circulose,” Renewcell stated on its website. “With Altor’s ownership, there is secure financing for the future of Circulose, ensuring that the company’s pioneering cotton recycling technology continues to thrive on a global scale.” (Re)vive has raised $3.5 million in a Seed round led by Equal Ventures and Hustle Fund with participation from Banter Capital, Coalition Operators, Mute VC, Veronica Chou, Charge VC, Everywhere VC, and Hyphen Capital. The New York-based company offers a “pioneering solution [aimed at] addressing the challenges of unstockable and returned inventory for future-minded brands.” Fashion brands are “grappling with mounting operational costs associated with processing, storing, and disposing returns, which can amount to as much as $15+ per item,” said Allison Lee, founder and CEO of (Re)vive. “However, with a growing demand for sustainable fashion from consumers, we see a huge opportunity for future-minded brands to leverage their once-disposed, damaged product into a coveted item.” Syre has raised $100 million in a Series A round led by founding investor TPG Rise Climate, which was joined by an additional investment from founder H&M Group, as well as Giant Ventures, IMAS Foundation, Norrsken VC, and Volvo Cars. The Stockholm-based textile impact company will use the new funds to finance the construction of its blueprint plant in the U.S., which will be up and running later this year, as well as preparations to establish the company’s first two gigascale textile-to-textile recycling plants. “I am thrilled that some of the most ambitious investors globally have joined our quest to lead the great textile shift. It’s inspiring to see their commitment to drive the green transition of the textile industry, across our key target industry verticals apparel, automotive, and interior,” says Dennis Nobelius, CEO of Syre. Silana has raised €1.5 million in a new funding round led by SOSV with participation from the HAX accelerator, OÖ HightechFonds, tech investor Material V, waterdrop founders Martin & Henry Murray, textile sustainability expert Yoobin Jung, and Sequoia Scout and former N26 CGO Alexander Weber. The Michael Hofmannrichter, Anton Wohlgemuth, and Michael Mayr-founded company will use the new funds to accelerate development of its sewing robot, with the aim of delivering the first machines next year.
