Once among the most important couturiers in the 1920s and early 1930s, the house helped define a modern vision of the female wardrobe before receding into decades of diminished visibility following Jean Patou’s death in 1936. What endured was fragrance licensing, anchored by the JOY perfume launched in 1929, preserving the Patou name in consumer consciousness even as the brand itself largely vanished from commerce. Over that period of dormancy, the U.S. trademark register came to quietly reflect the shift. Third-party owned registrations for marks like JOY CULT, JOYLAND, BODYJOY, JOYMEET, and JOY ENVIE accumulated across cosmetics, wellness, fragrance-adjacent goods, and lifestyle categories. In the absence of an active party policing unauthorized use of Patou’s JOY mark on fragrances, third parties treated “joy” as fair game, a perception reinforced as even sophisticated companies adopted JOY-based branding for beauty and fragrance goods. Fast forward and that disconnect between Jean Patou’s legacy and the brand’s activity has come to shape Patou’s modern trademark reckoning, much of which centers on the word “JOY.” The roots of Patou’s modern enforcement strategy lie in its acquisition by LVMH . In 2018, LVMH acquired Jean Patou in what the media described as a “stealth” transaction, with the French group taking control of the brand and its intellectual property from UK-based licensee Designer Parfums. Former Dior CEO and LVMH Fashion Group chairman Sidney Toledano took on the role of chairman of Patou’s board, and Guillaume Henry, previously creative director at Carven and Nina Ricci, was appointed to relaunch women’s ready-to-wear. By 2019, the house formally reintroduced itself simply as “Patou,” positioning the revival as both a heritage reclamation and a modern luxury reboot. The timing was not coincidental. Just one year earlier, LVMH-owned Dior had launched a fragrance named JOY – the same name as Patou’s historic perfume – an overlap that became largely frictionless once Patou entered the LVMH portfolio. But beneath the branding narrative, a quieter and more consequential legal campaign was already underway. Beginning in 2019, Patou dramatically increased its activity before the U.S. Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (“TTAB”), filing a steady stream of oppositions and procedural filings targeted at applications for JOY-centric trademarks. Notably, Patou does not appear to be pursuing U.S. infringement litigation in federal court. Instead, its enforcement posture is concentrated almost entirely on blocking others’ attempts to register JOY-centric marks at the USPTO – from names such as JOYROSE, JOYNOW, and JOY 101 to phrases like “A LITTLE JOY, EVERY DAY” for use on perfumes, cosmetics, and wellness products. Importantly, not every filing in the dataset has matured into a fully-prosecuted opposition. A meaningful subset consists of Requests for Extension of Time to Oppose, procedural mechanisms that allow a rights holder to preserve its ability to assess a potentially conflicting application before deciding whether to initiate a formal challenge. Even so, the combined volume of extensions and oppositions reflects a material uptick in monitoring and early-intervention posture – consistent with a portfolio recalibration following the LVMH acquisition. While many of the opposed applications come from foreign manufacturers or early-stage consumer startups, the docket also includes recognizable corporate actors, including CVS Pharmacy, Walmart, Amazon, Ulta Beauty, Unilever, and Philosophy, which reveals that Patou’s enforcement strategy extends to relatively low-stakes targets and commercially significant brand owners, alike. LVMH’s acquisition has functioned as a reset moment. What the group inherited was not merely a dormant brand and an archive, but a trademark asset whose exclusivity had been structurally eroded by years of under-enforcement. But reasserting control over JOY has required more than creative direction and retail rollout. Behind the scenes, consistent legal action is angling to restore order to a trademark landscape that had grown crowded during the brand’s absence. Against this background, the post-2019 opposition surge resembles a delayed market correction. LVMH appears to be drawing a hard boundary around a word the industry had grown accustomed to borrowing freely, signaling that JOY is not a generic mood descriptor in fragrance, but a mark with a single, identifiable source. This framing also explains why the enforcement program is tilted toward registry control rather than courtroom litigation. The objective does not appear to be damages or injunctions against isolated sellers; it is about controlling who can register and use the word as a trademark. Each JOY-prefixed mark on the register reduces Patou’s ability to preserve exclusivity as it rebuilds the brand globally. That strategy has already found validation both in opposition proceedings before the TTAB and in court outside the United States. In April 2024, the General Court of the European Union, for instance, upheld the EUIPO’s refusal to register a third-party’s “Joyful by Nature” mark following an opposition brought by Patou. The court reaffirmed that Patou’s JOY mark retains reputation despite periods of dormancy, recognizing that trademark reputation erodes gradually and can persist even when active commercial use is in flux. In doing so, the court effectively validated the logic behind Patou’s broader enforcement push: that JOY still functions as a source-identifying mark in fragrance and beauty. Reviving a heritage fashion house has always been an intensive and high-risk exercise. The fashion industry is filled with failed resurrection attempts – from Halston and Charles James to Helmut Lang. But LVMH’s historical playbook – which includes Moynat, Givenchy , Dior , etc. – suggests that legal infrastructure is as important as creative revival. Before a brand can scale product, retail, and licensing, it must reclaim control over the marks that make its name economically meaningful. Patou’s opposition-heavy strategy reflects that logic. By policing the register aggressively and early, LVMH is not merely looking to protect the name of a perfume. It is reasserting legal control over a word that had become widely used – and more than that, it is laying the groundwork for a significant luxury revival. Share

article_title: The Top U.S. Law Schools for Fashion Law
sub_title: Choosing the best law school for fashion law is critical for students aiming to pursue careers in this competitive legal specialty.
article_content: Choosing the best law school for fashion law is critical for students aiming to pursue careers in this competitive legal specialty. The Fashion Law’s editorial team – composed of lawyers and legal analysts – has identified the top U.S. law schools offering fashion law programs, courses, certificates, and other pathways into fashion and retail law careers. Not a single discipline, fashion law is a multidisciplinary practice area that spans intellectual property , commercial and corporate law, employment law, international trade, finance, technology and data privacy, and ESG , and encompasses critical legal issues, such as brand protection, licensing , advertising, privacy, and labor rights. As the fashion industry continues to evolve amid globalization, digital commerce, and shifting consumer expectations, demand for lawyers specialized in these intersecting areas has only intensified. When considering a program, prospective students should assess factors like experiential learning opportunities, geographic proximity to fashion hubs, faculty expertise, alumni career paths, and access to externships or industry-facing initiatives. It is also crucial to evaluate which subfields of the broad arena of “fashion law” – whether intellectual property , labor and employment, ESG compliance, mergers and acquisitions , international trade, etc. – align most closely with one’s interests and career ambitions. New York City continues to anchor fashion law education in the United States. But the presence of programs in Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., and Dallas reflects a broader shift in where fashion’s legal, regulatory, and commercial issues are being shaped. Each of the institutions highlighted below offers dedicated academic programming and a student-led fashion law society, underscoring institutional commitment and a growing student demand for legal careers at the intersection of creativity and commerce. Brooklyn Law School integrates fashion law into its broader strengths in business, intellectual property, and commercial law. Located in Downtown Brooklyn, the school features a dedicated Fashion Law course that examines the core legal issues and commercial challenges facing the U.S. fashion and retail industries, and how those dynamics shape legal practice. Complementing the academic curriculum, Brooklyn Law’s student-run Fashion Law Society hosts an annual Fashion Law Symposium, bringing together industry experts to address topics such as intellectual property, sustainability, and brand protection. Cardozo School of Law is home to the FAME Center (Fashion, Arts, Media & Entertainment), a program purpose-built to prepare students for legal careers across the fashion, arts, media, and entertainment industries. Based in New York City, Cardozo pairs a nationally recognized intellectual property program with hands-on learning, placing students in externships with leading brands and institutions such as Estée Lauder, the Brooklyn Nets, Burberry, Chanel, David Yurman, SoulCycle, and the Whitney Museum of American Art. Through fashion-law-focused coursework, its 11-year-old FAME program – led by fashion law pioneer Barbara Kolsun – and an active, student-run Fashion Law Society, Cardozo emphasizes the cross-disciplinary training required to navigate today’s increasingly complex fashion ecosystem. Columbia Law School supports fashion law through a robust intellectual property curriculum and the Kernochan Center for Law, Media, and the Arts. Located in New York, Columbia is also home to the Visual Arts Infringement Database, a widely used resource that highlights infringement issues and case law in the visual arts for students, artists, and practitioners. Complementing these academic resources, Columbia’s Fashion Law Society connects students pursuing fashion-focused legal careers through professional, educational, and social programming addressing topics ranging from intellectual property and labor to sustainability and the global fashion business. Fordham University School of Law is a pioneer in the field of fashion law.  In 2010, it launched the Fashion Law Institute, the first academic center dedicated exclusively to fashion law. The Institute offers more than 15 specialized fashion law courses covering topics from licensing and retail law to sustainability, international trade, and in-house counsel roles. Located in Manhattan, Fordham Law offers the world’s first M.S.L. and LL.M. degrees in Fashion Law, as well as the annual Fashion Law Bootcamp led by Professor Susan Scafidi. Students can gain exposure to the fashion industry and opportunities to connect with leading fashion companies. Harvard Law School supports the study of fashion law through a combination of specialized coursework and active student-led organizations. Located in Cambridge, Massachusetts, Harvard offers the Fashion Law Lab, developed by Nana Sarian and run with Rebecca Harris. The Lab is structured as a series of interactive, case-study-driven workshops that examine fashion law through a problem-based lens, drawing on litigation, corporate, and intellectual property frameworks, and welcoming key speakers from across the retail industry. The Harvard Fashion Law Association and the Harvard Art Law Organization also serve as focal points for students interested in the fashion and art industries, convening practitioners, academics, and students through programming, discussion, and professional networking. Howard University School of Law offers a policy- and practice-oriented foundation well suited to students interested in fashion law at the intersection of intellectual property, business, and regulation. Located in Washington, D.C., Howard’s strong emphasis on civil rights, labor and employment law, and international and comparative law provides a relevant framework for addressing issues central to the fashion industry, including supply-chain labor practices, consumer protection, and brand governance. In addition to relevant coursework, Howard boasts a student-led Fashion Law Society, which facilitates programming and discussion around fashion-related legal issues. New York Law School provides formal training in fashion law through specialized coursework, practice-based instruction, and student-led organizations. Located in New York City, the school’s Fashion Law Initiative integrates classroom instruction with exposure to real-world legal practice, offering students opportunities for focused study, research, and direct engagement with in-house and external counsel for leading fashion brands. Central to this framework is the Fashion Law Practicum, a practice-oriented course that examines the core dimensions of fashion law, including litigation strategy and transactional counseling, and is designed to prepare students for legal roles within fashion companies. Outside the classroom, students can further engage with the field through the Media, Entertainment, and Fashion Law Association, which provides professional development and industry networking. New York University School of Law’s strengths in corporate, intellectual property, and transactional law provide a strong foundation for fashion-focused legal careers. Based in Manhattan, NYU offers elective coursework addressing fashion law and business, hosts industry-facing events, and draws on a faculty with deep expertise in fashion law, intellectual property, and retail regulation, many of whom regularly publish on key developments in the field. The school also supports student engagement through its student-led Fashion Law Society, which complements the academic program with professional programming and networking opportunities. Southern Methodist University Dedman School of Law has emerged as an up-and-coming institution in fashion law education, particularly at the intersection of intellectual property, retail, and consumer goods law. Based in Dallas, Texas, the school offers dedicated coursework in fashion law and sneaker law. Student interest in the field is further supported by its Intellectual Property Organization, along with brand protection and IP practice-focused speaker events. A key component of SMU’s fashion law education is its corporate externship program, which places students in in-house legal roles at companies such as JCPenney, LTK, and Neiman Marcus. The University of Miami School of Law situates fashion law within its broader focus on entertainment, arts, and sports law, reflecting the school’s proximity to creative and consumer-driven industries. Located in Coral Gables, Florida, the law school offers specialized coursework in fashion law and sneaker law and hosts the Counseling Creators Conference, which brings together participants from across the fashion and creative sectors for negotiation competitions and practice-oriented legal workshops. Students can further engage with the field through the school’s student-led Fashion Law Society, which supports professional development and industry-focused programming. University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School offers a business- and policy-oriented foundation relevant to students interested in fashion law at the intersection of intellectual property, corporate governance, antitrust, and consumer protection. Located in Philadelphia, Penn’s close integration with the Wharton School enables interdisciplinary exposure to retail, branding, and global supply-chain dynamics, while its strengths in IP and competition law provide a framework for addressing issues central to the fashion industry, including brand strategy, market power, and commercialization. Penn also has a student-led Fashion Law Society, which facilitates content around fashion- and retail-related legal issues. Villanova’s John F. Scarpa Center for Entrepreneurship and Law offers students a unique curriculum combining legal theory with commercial practice, focusing on the intersection of business and law. The school, which is based in Villanova, Pennsylvania, hosts an annual Fashion Law Symposium sponsored by the Fashion Law Society and the Scarpa Center, featuring in-house counsel from leading fashion companies. Villanova Law offers a course in fashion law, which examines the legal and business issues facing fashion and apparel companies, including IP, licensing, employment, retail, and global commercial challenges. The Fashion Law Society provides students with networking opportunities, events with industry experts, and runs a blog, The Fashion Verdict, focused on fashion law topics. As fashion law continues to evolve into a widely recognized and increasingly consequential legal discipline, these institutions are playing a central role in training the attorneys who will help define the legal landscape of the global fashion industry. Share

article_title: From Dupes to Disclosure: How the Law Is Catching Up with Influencers
sub_title: EU law also requires disclosure of any compensation earned by influencers in connection with promotional content.
article_content: The rise of “ dupe culture ” has reshaped product marketing across fashion, beauty and beyond, as influencers increasingly promote low-cost alternatives to luxury – and other high-end – goods with viral appeal. Yet, while the term “ dupe ” may signal affordability and trendiness to consumers, its promotion, particularly through influencer-led content, has drawn the attention of regulators and courts in Europe. At the center of the legal conversation is whether influencer-led dupe promotion crosses the line from marketing to misrepresentation. While dupes may avoid infringing trademarks or trade dress , legal concerns often arise from the messaging surrounding them . When influencers suggest that a budget product is identical to a luxury item, or imply equivalence through aesthetic, sensory, or performance-based claims, those representations could give rise to legal exposure. The growing reliance on influencer-driven comparisons, particularly when undisclosed or unverified, has prompted regulators to examine whether these practices mislead consumers or unfairly leverage the reputation of better-known brands. In the European Union, influencer marketing is governed by the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (“UCPD”), the principal consumer protection law across the single market. It prohibits misleading practices that distort consumer decision-making, whether through false information or the omission of material facts. This includes product comparisons, performance claims, and any undisclosed sponsorships. This framework has direct implications for dupe marketing, where claims of luxury-level performance must be objectively substantiated. Without such verification, influencers risk misleading consumers and incurring liability under the UCPD. EU law also requires disclosure of any compensation – monetary, in-kind, or commission-based – earned by influencers in connection with promotional content. Failure to do so may constitute unlawful advertising and expose both influencers and brands to national enforcement. In the U.S., similar obligations arise under the Federal Trade Commission Act and state-level false advertising laws. The FTC requires influencers to clearly and conspicuously disclose any material connection to a brand, including payments, free products, or affiliate links. Beyond disclosure, influencers may also face liability under federal and state false advertising laws if they misrepresent a product’s qualities or imply unfounded equivalence to a well-known brand. Regulators are increasingly attentive not only to product endorsements but to the broader messaging strategies that shape consumer expectations. In the context of dupe culture, where much of the appeal hinges on associations with well-known luxury brands, the influencer’s role in shaping those associations is increasingly central to emerging liability frameworks. This pan-European scrutiny has been especially pronounced in Italy, where recent enforcement actions have triggered legal reforms targeting influencer behavior. Chiara Ferragni’s high-profile legal battle over misleading charitable marketing – though not dupe-related – has become a flashpoint for influencer accountability. Following fines from Italy’s competition authority and the opening of a criminal fraud case, Ferragni’s case accelerated reforms requiring prominent digital creators to register with regulators and comply with stricter advertising and disclosure laws. In response, the Italian Council of Ministers approved the DDL Beneficenza, a draft law introducing new transparency rules for campaigns tied to charitable causes. Brands and influencers would be required to disclose on product packaging and in related marketing: the recipient of proceeds; the purpose of the donation; and the total donation amount or per-unit contribution. These disclosures must also be submitted in advance to AGCM, with follow-up reporting after the donation deadline. Fines for noncompliance range from €5,000 to €50,000, with the potential for business suspension in serious or repeat cases. Though still in draft form, the law reinforces Italy’s broader push to regulate commercial storytelling that leans on emotional appeal or cause-based marketing. In parallel, communications authority Agcom issued new guidelines in January 2024 targeting high-reach influencers, those with one million followers, high engagement, and a track record of paid content. Under these rules, such creators are treated as Audiovisual Media Services, akin to traditional broadcasters under Italian media law. The guidelines require influencers to clearly disclose all sponsored content (e.g., using #adv), respect human dignity, avoid subliminal advertising, and comply with protections for minors. They also introduce editorial responsibility, obliging influencers to verify claims, cite sources, and avoid spreading misinformation. Penalties for violations range from €10,000 to €600,000 depending on the infraction. While limited in scope for now, Agcom has indicated the framework may expand – potentially bringing a broader range of influencer activity under regulatory scrutiny. Agcom’s approach signals a broader shift: influencer content – regardless of tone or platform – is now subject to the same scrutiny as traditional advertising. THE BIGGER PICTURE : Taken together, the legal landscape across Europe suggests that influencer-driven dupe marketing cannot rely on informal norms or assumed good faith. As regulatory frameworks across the EU evolve, the days of informal or ambiguous influencer endorsements – particularly in dupe marketing – are quickly fading. Influencers and brands alike are being held to standards that demand transparency, substantiation, and legal compliance. Share

article_title: Estée Lauder Brands Sue Walmart Over Alleged Sale of Counterfeit Goods
sub_title: A group of Estée Lauder-owned companies has filed a trademark infringement lawsuit against Walmart, alleging that the retail titan sold counterfeit and
article_content: A group of Estée Lauder-owned companies has filed a trademark infringement lawsuit against Walmart, alleging that the retail titan sold counterfeit and otherwise infringing versions of its beauty and fragrance products through its online marketplace. In the newly-filed suit, the cosmetics brands allege that Walmart and its e-commerce subsidiary facilitated the sale of non-genuine products bearing the trademarks of Estée Lauder, Clinique, La Mer, Le Labo, Aveda, and Tom Ford. The case joins a growing number of disputes applying established marketplace liability precedent to increasingly integrated e-commerce platforms. In the complaint that it filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on February 9, the Estée Lauder Companies-owned brands (collectively, “ELC brands”) maintain that it purchased cosmetics products from Walmart.com and determined that they were not genuine items. The allegedly infringing products include skincare and fragrance items that make use of its trademark-protected brand names and in some cases, resemble well-known offerings, such as Estée Lauder’s Advanced Night Repair serum, Le Labo’s Santal 33 fragrance, La Mer’s moisturizers, and fragrances sold under the Tom Ford brand. The ELC brands assert that they have not authorized Walmart or the relevant marketplace sellers to use their trademarks in connection with these goods and argue that the sale of non-genuine products is likely to cause consumer confusion regarding the source, sponsorship, or approval of the products. At the heart of the trademark infringement, false designation of origin, trade dress infringement, and related unfair competition claims at play is Walmart.com’s third-party marketplace model. Like other major retailers, Walmart operates an online platform where outside sellers can list products alongside goods sold directly by Walmart. Distinguishing the case at hand from others, the ELC brands argue, is Walmart’s involvement in the marketplace, which it claims extends beyond merely hosting listings. Specifically (and in furtherance of its bid to establish direct and/or vicarious trademark liability), the ELC brands allege that Walmart “selects” and “partners” with marketplace sellers and controls key aspects of the transaction process for goods sold on its marketplace, including checkout, payment processing, customer service, fulfillment services, and returns. Consumers purchasing items through the marketplace may return products to Walmart stores, and customer service interactions are handled through Walmart’s systems. The ELC brands contend that this level of integration could lead consumers to believe they are purchasing directly from Walmart, even when a third-party seller is involved. Beyond that, the brands further allege that Walmart uses its search functionality and listing infrastructure to promote products bearing the ELC brands’ trademarks, thereby driving traffic to allegedly infringing goods and generating revenue and profits that “they would have not realized but for the defendants’ contributory infringement.” In short : The ELC brands claim that Walmart’s operational control over its marketplace makes it legally responsible for trademark infringement occurring through third-party sellers. At its core, the case is about who bears responsibility when alleged counterfeits are sold on a major U.S. retail platform? Hardly novel territory, the newly-filed suit fits within an established body of case law addressing when an online marketplace may be liable for infringing goods sold by third parties. Courts, including the Second Circuit in Tiffany (NJ) Inc. v. eBay Inc. (applying the Supreme Court’s framework in Inwood Laboratories, Inc. v. Ives Laboratories, Inc. ), have held that marketplaces may be contributorily liable if they have specific knowledge of particular infringing listings or sellers and continue to provide services without taking appropriate action. More recent cases have examined not only knowledge-based contributory liability under Inwood, but also whether a platform’s operational involvement in the transaction – including control over listings, payment processing, fulfillment, customer service, and returns – may support theories of direct or vicarious trademark liability. In particular, courts have considered whether such integration reflects sufficient “use in commerce” or a degree of control and financial interest consistent with vicarious liability principles. Here, the ELC brands emphasize Walmart’s alleged control over checkout and payment processing, its handling of returns (including in-store returns), and its provision of fulfillment and customer service. With that in mind, the case is likely to turn on a fact-intensive assessment of Walmart’s level of control and whether that involvement is sufficient under existing precedent to support direct, contributory, or vicarious trademark liability. As major retailers continue expanding hybrid models that combine first-party sales with third-party marketplace offerings, disputes like this one highlight the ongoing tensions between brand protection efforts and the operational structure of large e-commerce platforms. The case is Estée Lauder Inc. et al., v. Walmart Inc. et al., 2:26-cv-01341 (C.D. Cal.). Share

article_title: Fashion Law in 2026: Navigating IP, ESG & the New Consumer
sub_title: To help professionals understand and adapt to this changing terrain, TFL is offering an upd virtual program: Fashion Law Fundamentals.
article_content: As fashion continues to evolve under the pressures of rapid digitization, changing consumer behaviors and preferences, and global regulatory reform, the legal frameworks that govern the industry are being tested and redefined. From intellectual property protection in the age of AI-generated design to the rise of resale and rework culture, the legal issues shaping fashion today are more complex, interdisciplinary, and consequential than ever. Fashion law – once a niche area of practice – is now central to how brands are built, protected, and scaled. At one end of the spectrum, luxury conglomerates are intensifying legal strategies to assert dominance over their intellectual property portfolios, vigorously defending trademarks, proprietary designs, and even digital assets as fashion intersects more deeply with technology. At the other, a new generation of independent designers and agile startups is operating at the edges of established IP doctrine, leveraging fair use, remix culture, and circular design practices like upcycling to differentiate themselves in saturated markets. At the heart of this shift lies a set of overlapping issues and trends … As dupes proliferate, AI-generated works flood the market , and consumers increasingly customize products, traditional models of intellectual property enforcement are showing strain. In response, brands are making use of on a new playbook to protect their creative and commercial assets , often pushing existing doctrines into unsettled territory. The rapid growth of resale has surfaced complex legal questions around trademark exhaustion, authentication, product modification, and brand affiliation. While some companies have embraced resale as part of a circular strategy, others have turned to litigation to assert control over how their products are marketed and resold. Courts in both the U.S. and EU are now grappling with platform liability and the boundaries of permissible secondary-market activity. The fashion and retail market is undergoing a period of acute instability, shaped by slowing demand, shifting consumer values, and mounting operational pressure. Longstanding brand narratives built on heritage , craftsmanship, and prestige are increasingly being tested by labor disputes and scrutiny of working conditions , forcing companies to reconcile brand mythology with on-the-ground realities. At the same time, evolving tariff regimes and trade restrictions are reshaping sourcing strategies, pricing structures, and global distribution models. These forces are not only squeezing margins but also complicating how brands present themselves to consumers, as economic policy, supply chain decisions, and labor practices become inseparable from brand identity and legal risk. The rise of reworked, customized, and upcycled fashion is testing the outer limits of IP law. Courts are being asked to decide whether these altered goods constitute transformative expression or actionable infringement, rulings that will shape the future of creative reuse and secondary markets. Sustainability has moved from branding rhetoric to legal exposure. Expanding ESG regulations , greenwashing enforcement , and supply-chain transparency laws are forcing companies to substantiate environmental and ethical claims or face growing litigation, regulatory risk, and reputational fallout. To help professionals understand and adapt to this changing terrain, TFL is offering a virtual program : Fashion Law Fundamentals. Designed for lawyers, designers, executives, influencers, entrepreneurs, and students, alike, participants will gain an unparalleled understanding of … > Intellectual Property Principles & Practice : An in-depth look at how fashion and retail brands protect design, trademarks, and brand identity in a global, digital marketplace increasingly shaped by dupes. The session covers trade dress and copyright enforcement, the interaction between IP and sustainability and resale, and how heritage functions as both a branding asset and an enforcement tool. > Emerging Issues in Fashion Law : A survey of the fast-moving legal issues reshaping fashion and retail, including resale and circularity, AI and design, influencer marketing, sustainability claims, and global enforcement. Using recent disputes and real-world examples, the session examines how intellectual property, consumer protection, technology, and regulatory law increasingly overlap in practice. > ESG & Consumer Protection: Navigating Regulation & Reputation : A practical examination of the legal risks facing consumer brands, from greenwashing and PFAS regulation to “Made in the USA” claims, labeling requirements, automatic renewals, and warranties. The session explores how lawyers assess risk, defend high-profile claims, and advise brands in a closely regulated and litigation-heavy environment. > Fashion Law in Practice : A candid, real-world perspective on practicing fashion law at the highest level, featuring a conversation with Lisa Keith, EVP, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of Steve Madden, Ltd. The session focuses on career paths, day-to-day legal decision-making, and the evolving role of IP, litigation, and brand protection in fashion and footwear businesses. As fashion becomes more interconnected and legally sophisticated, a deep and dynamic understanding of these issues is critical. Whether protecting a brand, launching a new line, or ensuring compliance across jurisdictions, legal fluency in fashion is a powerful asset in a competitive and regulated marketplace. Share

article_title: Legal Blitz Over Trump Tariffs: Inside e.l.f. and Ferragamo’s Lawsuits
sub_title: As SCOTUS weighs whether the president can lawfully impose tariffs under emergency powers, more than 1,000 companies have filed lawsuits.
article_content: As the U.S. Supreme Court weighs whether the president can lawfully impose tariffs under emergency powers, more than 1,000 companies have filed lawsuits challenging the Trump administration’s trade measures – and seeking refunds that could total billions of dollars. Two of those cases, filed by Ferragamo USA Inc. and e.l.f. Cosmetics, Inc., offer a close look at the legal strategy behind this growing wave of litigation. Ferragamo’s complaint – filed with the U.S. Court of International Trade on January 9 – targets tariffs imposed under a series of 2025 executive orders issued by President Donald Trump and grounded in the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”). The American arm of the Italian fashion company argues that the statute does not authorize the imposition of tariffs and that, without swift judicial relief, importers risk losing their ability to recover duties already paid, even if the Supreme Court ultimately strikes the tariffs down. A similar theory is the basis for the complaint filed a few days earlier by e.l.f. Cosmetics, which also challenges the legality of IEEPA-based tariffs and seeks declaratory and injunctive relief, along with full refunds of duties already paid. Like Ferragamo, e.l.f. alleges that it is an importer of record that has paid (and continues to pay) tariffs imposed pursuant to executive orders that courts have already found exceed the president’s statutory authority. Ferragamo’s and e.l.f.’s lawsuits are part of a much broader legal campaign. Publicly traded companies, including Costco Wholesale Corp., EssilorLuxottica SA, Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., Dole Fresh Fruit Co., and J. Crew Group LLC, are among the plaintiffs challenging the tariffs. The lawsuits target duties imposed under emergency authority that the government says generated roughly $133 billion as of mid-December, paid by more than 301,000 importers across some 34 million shipments. The scale of the collections – and the potential for mass refunds – helps explain why companies are racing to lodge claims before the Supreme Court issues its decision. Both the Ferragamo and e.l.f. cases illustrate a central concern animating the current wave of tariff litigation: timing. Although the Court of International Trade and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit have already held that IEEPA does not authorize the imposition of tariffs – most notably in V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. Trump – the two companies emphasize that those rulings do not guarantee refunds for importers that have already paid the duties. As both complaints underscore, once Customs “liquidates” an entry, importers may lose the legal ability to recover unlawfully collected duties, even if the underlying tariff regime is later invalidated, absent timely judicial relief. Against that backdrop, Ferragamo and e.l.f. assert that even a favorable Supreme Court ruling may come too late for companies that did not bring their own actions before liquidation occurs. With that in mind, both seek immediate declaratory and injunctive relief, including suspension of liquidation and orders requiring refunds of IEEPA duties with interest, to ensure that any eventual decision by the Supreme Court has concrete financial effect, rather than leaving recovery to uncertain post hoc administrative processes. If the Court strikes down the tariffs, the government could face unprecedented repayment claims. The Ferragamo and e.l.f. filings underscore that companies are not waiting to find out whether refunds will be automatic; they are suing in advance to secure them. For fashion and beauty companies , which rely heavily on global supply chains, the disputed tariffs translated into immediate cost increases. Economists have linked the measures to higher importer costs, inflationary pressure, weaker manufacturing activity, and slower growth, with U.S. consumers facing the highest effective tariff rate since 1935. Against that background, the Ferragamo and e.l.f. lawsuits reflect how businesses in fashion, beauty, and consumer goods are using the courts not only to challenge the legality of the tariffs, but to ensure that if the Supreme Court rules in their favor, they will actually get their money back. The Supreme Court heard oral argument on November 5 in consolidated challenges to President Trump’s authority to impose sweeping tariffs through a series of 2025 executive orders but has yet to issue a decision. While the dispute has drawn intense attention from businesses paying billions of dollars in duties each month, the Court has given no indication that it views the case as an emergency – suggesting that a ruling may follow the Court’s ordinary opinion-writing timeline rather than an accelerated schedule. The cases are Ferragamo USA Inc. v. U.S. , 1:26-cv-00504 (USCIT) and e.l.f. Cosmetics, Inc. v. U.S. , 1:26-cv-00049 (USCIT). Share

article_title: Fashion & Retail Funding and M&A Tracker
sub_title: Here is a running timeline of the most notable fashion, retail, activewear, and luxury-focused M&A and investments.
article_content: M&A and investments continue to dominate the fashion and luxury industries, with a rise in deal volume driven by ongoing consolidation, digital acceleration, and rising pressure on margins. From strategic acquisitions to tech-driven funding rounds, the landscape is increasingly shaped by players aiming to future-proof their operations and expand global reach. Big-name deals over the past several years have brought Tiffany & Co. under the umbrella of LVMH (after the two companies managed to put their rival lawsuits to bed and come to agreeable terms under which French conglomerate could acquire the famed New York-based jewelry stalwart); ridded Richemont of loss-making Yoox Net-a-Porter ; and saw Farfetch acquired in a rescue deal by Korea e-commerce giant Coupang. These moves come amid growing urgency around consolidation, with giants like LVMH, Kering, and Richemont sharpening their portfolios and tech stacks. Sources close to recent transactions suggest more tie-ups are in the pipeline, especially as mid-sized brands and service providers look for scale or exit opportunities in a high-cost, high-competition environment. “Whether it’s automation, data-driven pricing, or owning more of the value chain, the current deal flow shows the industry’s pivot toward resilience and agility,” says one sector analyst. As fashion grapples with evolving consumer behavior, cost pressures, and digital disruption, the M&A and funding landscape is set to remain active well into 2025 and beyond. With the foregoing in mind, here is a tracker of the most recent fashion and retail-focused M&A and investments … Samsonite Group agreed to acquire an 85% stake in Béis, the travel and luggage brand founded by actress and entrepreneur Shay Mitchell, for $178.5 million, valuing the company at $210 million. The acquisition expands Samsonite’s portfolio of travel brands, which includes TUMI, High Sierra and Gregory. Founded in 2018, Béis generated approximately $210 million in net sales in 2025. Mitchell will remain chief creative officer and retain a 15% stake, while majority shareholder Beach House Group will sell its 70% interest. Samsonite plans to leverage its global distribution, sourcing and logistics capabilities to accelerate Béis’ growth while maintaining the brand as a standalone business. “Joining the Samsonite Group gives us the chance to dream even bigger,” said Shay Mitchell, founder and chief creative officer of Béis. Frasers Group acquired luxury department store Harvey Nichols out of administration for an undisclosed amount, ending 35 years of ownership by Hong Kong billionaire Dickson Poon. The transaction includes six UK stores, the company’s e-commerce operations, inventory and international franchise agreements, with more than 1,000 employees transferring to Frasers. The acquisition adds another prominent retail brand to Frasers’ portfolio, which includes House of Fraser, Evans Cycles and Sofa.com. Frasers plans to restructure Harvey Nichols to restore the loss-making retailer to sustainable growth, potentially reviewing its store footprint, organizational structure and cost base. “The turnaround will require tough choices, and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term,” said Michael Murray, CEO of Frasers Group. Scalpers has acquired a stake in Spanish youth fashion brand Yuxus to support its domestic and international expansion. Financial terms and the size of the stake were not disclosed. Yuxus, founded eight years ago by brothers Guillermo and Álvaro Ferre, operates 14 stores and employs nearly 100 people. The founders will remain involved in management, while Yuxus gains access to Scalpers’ resources to strengthen existing markets and enter new countries. The investment advances Scalpers’ strategy of building a portfolio of high-growth fashion brands, which already includes Victoria, Mim Shoes and Deeply. The transaction data comes from Dealroom.co, citing Forbes España as the original source. MondeVita has acquired a majority stake in Underscore District, the Milan-based brand accelerator behind Magliano, GR10K and WOK Store. Financial terms were not disclosed. The transaction follows MondeVita’s acquisition of menswear manufacturer Raffaele Caruso and adds brand development, merchandising, retail and e-commerce capabilities to its growing Italian luxury platform. Underscore District generated more than €7 million in sales in 2025 across a wholesale network of over 150 retailers. CEO Edoardo Di Luzio will remain in place and take on a broader strategic role within MondeVita, while the group plans to support Magliano’s international expansion and pursue additional luxury acquisitions. “We are building a platform where creativity and established craftsmanship reinforce one another, and Underscore District is central to that design,” said Fabio Brambilla, chairman of MondeVita. Canada Goose Holdings has agreed to sell Baffin Limited, its Canadian performance footwear brand, to L.P. Royer, a Canadian manufacturer of work and military footwear. Financial terms were not disclosed, and the transaction is expected to close in August, subject to customary closing conditions. Canada Goose acquired Baffin in 2018 as its first move into footwear, using the acquisition to build expertise and infrastructure as it expanded beyond outerwear. Founded in 1979, Baffin specializes in technical footwear designed for demanding environments and has established a strong reputation for performance, durability and Canadian craftsmanship. Under Royer’s ownership, the brand will join another long-established Canadian footwear manufacturer with expertise across industrial, mining, construction and military applications. “This transaction is about focus. We’ve made meaningful progress evolving Canada Goose into a year-round lifestyle brand, and this gives us the opportunity to continue that momentum by simplifying our operating model, focusing resources on our highest-priority opportunities and drive long-term profitable growth,” said Dani Reiss, Chairman & CEO of Canada Goose. WME Group has sold the New York Fashion Week, NYFW and NYFW: The Shows trademarks and intellectual property to Signet Fashion, including associated websites and social media assets. Financial terms were not disclosed. Signet plans to expand the NYFW platform through live programming, digital content, media production, brand partnerships and year-round audience engagement. “We welcome Signet’s investment and look forward to seeing how its efforts help create new opportunities for designers and contribute to the continued success of New York Fashion Week,” said Steven Kolb, President and CEO of the CFDA. LVMH has sold Patou to Nirvana Investments LLC-FZ, the holding company of Dubai-based entrepreneur and Designer Parfums founder Dilesh Mehta. Financial terms were not disclosed. LVMH originally acquired a majority stake in Patou from Mehta in 2018, with Mehta retaining a 30% interest, and subsequently relaunched the historic French maison as a fashion label after roughly three decades of dormancy in fashion. The transaction returns control of Patou to Mehta following a period of leadership changes, including the departures of CEO Sophie Brocart in 2024 and artistic director Guillaume Henry in February 2026. “We now look forward to building on that foundation and continuing Patou’s growth with the same long-term vision, respect for its heritage and ambition for the future,” said Dilesh Mehta. Crown Brands Group has acquired Italian luxury lingerie brand Cosabella from CALIDA GROUP, marking its second acquisition in seven months following the purchase of Hanky Panky. The deal expands Crown’s premium intimates portfolio and supports its strategy of acquiring heritage consumer brands with global growth potential. “Cosabella is everything we look for in a brand: true Italian craftsmanship, a devoted customer, and a name that means something in every major market,” said Raymond Dayan, CEO of Crown Brands Group. UK retailer Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28%, crossing the threshold under German takeover rules that requires a mandatory takeover offer. Frasers acquired an additional 2.55 million shares, up from its previous 26.06% holding, reinforcing its position as Hugo Boss’ largest shareholder. The move follows Frasers’ €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss urged shareholders to reject as “financially inadequate.” Frasers said its offer remains open through July 27. A Hugo Boss spokesperson said the increased shareholding “does not have any implications for the voluntary takeover offer or the offer process.” UK womenswear brand Never Fully Dressed has sold a minority stake to Refined Capital Partners in its first external investment since founder Lucy Aylen launched the business in 2009. Financial terms were not disclosed. The investment will support the brand’s future growth while allowing its existing leadership team to remain in place. Refined Capital Partners’ portfolio includes The Fold, Frugi, Disturbia, Celtic & Co, and Turtle Doves. In a statement, Never Fully Dressed described the deal as “an exciting milestone,” adding: “We’re still the same female-founded brand, led by the same leadership team, designing every print in-house with the same passion, creativity and attention to detail.” The company said the partnership will enable further investment in the business and strengthen its commitment to its people, sustainability efforts, and long-term expansion. French running retailer i-Run has acquired Belgian running and trail specialist Trakks, expanding its presence in the Benelux region. Founded by Christophe Thomas, Trakks operates six stores and an e-commerce platform, generating €7.1 million in revenue and €0.7 million in net profit in 2025. The acquisition will see Trakks rebranded as “Trakks by i-Run”, with integration into i-Run’s systems scheduled for October. Trakks’ founders will remain with the business for at least two years to support the transition and drive i-Run’s regional growth. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Chanel has acquired Charvet, the historic French luxury shirtmaker, strengthening a relationship that dates back to founder Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel, who famously purchased Charvet shirts for Arthur “Boy” Capel. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Founded in 1838, Charvet is renowned for its bespoke shirts and craftsmanship, employing around 100 people across its Paris flagship and French production workshop. The acquisition follows creative director Matthieu Blazy’s collaboration with Charvet on Chanel’s Spring 2026 collection, which featured oversized cotton shirts that became standout pieces of the season. Chanel said the deal will preserve Charvet’s heritage and craftsmanship while ensuring its long-term future. “We decided to get married. We thought it made sense for the future of Charvet to be secured by Chanel,” said Bruno Pavlovsky, President of Fashion and President of Chanel SAS. “It’s part of our legend and storytelling.” Damiani Group has completed its acquisition of Baume & Mercier from Richemont, adding the 200-year-old Swiss watchmaker to its portfolio of luxury jewelry and watch brands. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The acquisition strengthens Damiani’s position in hard luxury and expands its watchmaking business. The group plans to increase Baume & Mercier’s global visibility by leveraging its international distribution network and selectively opening mono-brand boutiques, while Richemont will continue providing operational support during the integration period. “The Damiani Group is uniquely positioned to realise Baume & Mercier’s full potential… We are confident to have found in Damiani Group the right home for Baume & Mercier to thrive in years to come,” said Nicolas Bos, Chief Executive Officer of Richemont. HSG has completed its acquisition of Italian luxury footwear brand Golden Goose, becoming the company’s majority shareholder in a deal that values the business at nearly $2.5 billion. Temasek is also joining the transaction as a strategic minority investor through True Light Capital. As part of the ownership transition, former Gucci chief Marco Bizzarri has been appointed non-executive chairman, effective immediately, while CEO Silvio Campara will remain in his role. The deal formalizes a transaction first announced last year and comes as Golden Goose continues to post growth, with first-quarter revenue rising 10% year over year to €173.2 million. Italian luxury group OTB has acquired the remaining stake in Viktor&Rolf, taking full ownership of the Dutch fashion house founded by Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren. Financial terms were not disclosed. OTB first acquired a majority stake in Viktor&Rolf in 2008 and increased its ownership to 70% in 2019. The transaction completes OTB’s long-term investment in the brand, while the founders will remain in place as creative directors under an agreement extended last year. Known for its avant-garde haute couture, ready-to-wear, bridalwear, eyewear, and fragrance business with L’Oréal Luxe, Viktor&Rolf becomes a wholly owned part of OTB’s luxury portfolio, which includes Diesel, Jil Sander, Maison Margiela, Marni, and Amiri. UK online flash-sales retailer BrandAlley has been rescued through a pre-pack administration deal, with the business, brand, website, and ongoing operations acquired by BrandAlley International Ltd. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The restructuring follows financial difficulties at BrandAlley and is expected to preserve the majority of operations. Of the company’s 163 employees, 15 have been made redundant, with approximately 60 additional roles expected to be affected following completion of the ownership transfer. According to the company, customer operations will continue uninterrupted, with existing orders, returns, and refunds being honored as normal. The deal secures the future of one of the UK’s best-known online off-price fashion and lifestyle retailers while allowing the business to continue trading under new ownership. Digital fashion startup Meta Fashion has raised approximately $400,000 in a pre-seed funding round led by Lumikai, with participation from investors including Big Bets, Anton Gauffin, Akshat Rathee, and Pratham Mittal. Founded in 2022 by Arjun Goel, the company develops digital fashion assets for platforms including Roblox, Fortnite, and ZEPETO, while also building its own Roblox-based game, GlamGirls. Meta Fashion said it has sold more than 2.5 million virtual fashion items on Roblox, generating nearly $300,000 in GMV. The company plans to use the funding to expand across UGC gaming platforms, scale its virtual fashion business, and grow its GlamGirls IP. Gordon Brothers has acquired British handbag and accessories brand Radley and its related intellectual property as part of its growing portfolio of heritage fashion and lifestyle brands. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in London’s Camden Market in 1998, Radley built a strong presence in accessible luxury through its handbags and accessories business. Gordon Brothers said it plans to pursue an asset-light, licensing-led growth strategy focused on expanding the brand across the U.S., U.K., Australia, and Asia while broadening categories beyond handbags into watches, jewelry, eyewear, and beauty gifting. “We are thrilled to add another British icon to our global portfolio of brands,” said Tobias Nanda, Head of Brands at Gordon Brothers. The acquisition further expands Gordon Brothers’ fashion brand portfolio, which already includes Nicole Miller, LK Bennett, Rachel Zoe, and Laura Ashley. Authentic Brands Group has signed a definitive agreement to acquire heritage denim label Lee from Kontoor Brands, further expanding its portfolio of global fashion and lifestyle brands. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded more than a century ago, Lee generates approximately $1.5 billion in annual retail sales across 73 countries. Following the acquisition, Authentic plans to transition the business to its licensing-driven operating model, leveraging its global network of partners to expand the brand across apparel, experiences, and lifestyle categories. “What makes Lee so compelling is its legacy,” said Authentic founder and executive chairman Jamie Salter. “It’s one of the most important names in denim.” The transaction is expected to close in the second half of 2026, subject to regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. Marquee Brands has signed a deal to acquire a majority interest in Roberto Cavalli through a strategic partnership with DAMAC Group, which will remain a significant shareholder. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition adds Roberto Cavalli to Marquee Brands’ growing portfolio of lifestyle and fashion brands and expands its presence in luxury fashion, bringing total portfolio-wide retail sales to approximately $5 billion. “Roberto Cavalli stands as one of luxury’s defining Italian houses,” said Marquee Brands CEO Heath Golden. As part of the transaction, Milan-based The Level Group will oversee product development, retail, e-commerce, and wholesale operations for the brand across Europe and the U.S. Artemis, the holding company controlled by the Pinault family and owner of Kering, has agreed to sell its majority stake in Giambattista Valli back to founder Giambattista Valli as part of a broader effort to streamline investments and reduce debt. Financial terms were not disclosed. The move follows Artemis’ recent sale of a 29% stake in Puma to Anta Sports Products for €1.5 billion earlier this year. “This agreement now allows me to regain full control of my brand,” Valli said in a statement. The transaction comes amid continued pressure across the luxury sector as weaker global demand weighs on independent high-end fashion brands. The s.Oliver Group has acquired the Baldessarini brand rights from New Baldessarini GmbH, a subsidiary of R.Brand Group, as part of its strategy to strengthen its premium menswear offering. Financial terms were not disclosed. Baldessarini will operate as an independent label within s.Oliver’s growing House of Brands portfolio alongside Lala Berlin, while helping expand the group’s position in contemporary tailoring and premium casualwear. “Baldessarini is a strong brand with great potential,” said s.Oliver Group co-CEO Johannes Rellecke. “With it, we are closing the gap between classic business wear and modern casual menswear.” The relaunch of Baldessarini under the s.Oliver umbrella is planned for early 2027. Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein is set to acquire direct-to-consumer apparel brand Everlane in a deal reportedly valued at around $100 million, according to reports. The transaction follows months of financial pressure at Everlane, which reportedly carried roughly $90 million in liabilities, including a $25 million loan from Gordon Brothers and a $65 million revolving credit facility. Majority shareholder L Catterton and CEO Alfred Chang had reportedly explored outside investment options before Shein opted for a full acquisition. Puck reported that holders of Everlane common stock are not expected to receive proceeds from the transaction, though details regarding preferred shareholders were not disclosed. The acquisition would give Shein ownership of a well-known U.S. contemporary fashion label as the company continues expanding beyond its fast-fashion roots and deepening its global retail footprint. LVMH has agreed to sell Marc Jacobs to a joint venture formed by WHP Global and G-III Apparel Group, with the buyers raising up to $850 million to finance the acquisition. Under the deal, WHP Global and G-III will each contribute up to $425 million, with WHP overseeing licensing operations and G-III managing the brand globally. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The sale marks the end of LVMH’s nearly 30-year ownership of Marc Jacobs, which it acquired in 1997. Founder Marc Jacobs will remain creative director following the transaction. The acquisition expands WHP Global’s premium fashion portfolio, which already includes Vera Wang, rag & bone, and G-STAR, while reflecting broader consolidation trends in the accessible luxury market. Castore has secured a £90 million credit facility from HSBC UK, BNP Paribas, and Lloyds to support retail expansion in the UK and accelerate growth across key international markets in the Middle East and Asia. The Manchester-based sportswear brand plans to use the financing to expand its store footprint and strengthen its position as a global premium performance apparel company. Castore is targeting more than £300 million in sales over the next financial year. “This new funding provides us with the flexibility and ability to accelerate our retail rollout,” said co-founder Tom Beahon. Founded in 2015, Castore has attracted backing from investors including Andy Murray and INEOS, and recently acquired heritage fashion brand Belstaff for approximately £102 million. Kering has announced it will acquire a minority stake in Shanghai-based Icicle Fashion Group as part of a strategic partnership with its parent company ICCF. Founded in 1997, Icicle is a fast-growing Chinese luxury brand with more than 200 stores globally, including a presence in Paris, and has been expanding into Western markets. The investment reflects Kering’s continued focus on strengthening its position in China while supporting the international growth of local luxury brands. Financial terms were not disclosed. Kering and L’Oréal have finalized their strategic beauty partnership, confirming L’Oréal’s €4 billion acquisition of Kering Beauté, including the House of Creed, along with long-term fragrance and beauty licenses for Kering’s luxury Houses. The agreement also includes plans to explore new opportunities in wellness and longevity through a joint venture, signaling a broader expansion beyond traditional beauty categories. “Our strategic alliance with L’Oréal marks a decisive step forward for Kering,” said CEO Luca de Meo. For L’Oréal, the deal strengthens its leadership in luxury beauty, building on its longstanding success with brands like Yves Saint Laurent Beauté while unlocking new growth opportunities across Kering’s portfolio. Perfect Moment has secured $12 million in growth financing to strengthen its balance sheet and support its path to sustainable profitability. The package includes a $10 million revolving credit facility from Krane Capital and X3 Higher Moment Fund, alongside a $2 million equity investment from Krane Capital, priced at a 75% premium to the company’s recent share price. The funding follows the brand’s first profitable quarter and will be used to enhance liquidity, invest in product innovation, and expand into new categories and markets. A key focus is China, where Krane Capital’s local expertise is expected to support distribution and market entry within the premium segment. “This financing enhances our financial flexibility and supports continued expansion across our key initiatives,” said Executive Chairman Max Gottschalk. American Exchange Group has agreed to acquire the assets of Allbirds in a $39 million deal, marking a dramatic reset for the once high-flying sustainable footwear brand. The transaction, expected to close in Q2 2026 pending shareholder approval, will include the winding down of Allbirds’ public company structure. The deal follows a sharp decline in performance, with the company reporting a 23.3% drop in quarterly revenue and continued losses, alongside the closure of its remaining U.S. stores. Originally launched in 2016 and once valued at over $4 billion, Allbirds rose quickly on the strength of its minimalist wool sneakers before struggling with rapid expansion and strategic missteps. “This next chapter… sets up the brand to thrive in the years ahead,” said CEO Joe Vernachio. For American Exchange Group, the acquisition adds to a growing portfolio of fashion and lifestyle brands, signaling continued consolidation in the footwear and apparel sector. Sandbridge Capital, a private equity firm focused on consumer and luxury investments, has taken a 5% stake in  Jacquemus. The transaction involves the sale of the founder’s personal shares, rather than new capital being injected into the business. It follows L’Oréal’s earlier investment of around 10%, supporting Jacquemus’ planned expansion into beauty, including a cosmetics line set to launch in 2027. Despite new investors, founder Simon Porte Jacquemus retains majority ownership. London-based fashion distributor and brand incubator Tomorrow Ltd. has been acquired by Progetto 11, the parent company of Italian e-commerce platform The Level Group. Financial terms were not disclosed, though existing investor Three Hills Capital Partners is reported to have taken a loss on its stake. Founded as a showroom business, Tomorrow evolved into a brand incubator with stakes in labels including Coperni and Martine Rose, supporting production, development, and distribution. However, the company has faced mounting challenges in recent years, including declining revenues, liquidity pressures, and tensions with partner brands. “The focus of the board has been to guarantee protection and continuity for the business,” said founder Stefano Martinetto. The acquisition is expected to stabilise operations and integrate Tomorrow into The Level Group’s broader e-commerce and logistics platform, though the future of its brand partnerships remains uncertain. French rainwear brand Flotte has raised €2.5 million in funding from Time4, a new investment fund launched by Daphni and Les Déterminés. The funding will support the brand’s growth and expansion as it continues to scale its sustainable outerwear offering. Founded as a specialist rainwear label, Flotte focuses on functional, eco-conscious apparel designed for urban lifestyles. Online retailer Quince has raised $500 million in a Series E funding round led by ICONIQ Capital, with participation from Basis Set Ventures and Wellington Management. The round values the company at $10.1 billion. The San Francisco–based platform sells apparel, jewelry, and home goods through a manufacturer-to-consumer model that removes traditional retail intermediaries. Its AI-driven platform forecasts demand and produces goods in smaller batches to reduce excess inventory. Quince reported more than $1 billion in revenue in 2025 and plans to use the new funding to support global expansion of its technology-enabled retail model. Frasers Group has acquired a 5.8% stake in German sportswear company Puma, according to regulatory filings. The position was largely built through derivatives tied to roughly 8.5 million shares. If exercised, the stake would make Frasers Puma’s second-largest shareholder behind the Pinault family. The move follows Anta Sports’ agreement earlier this year to purchase a 29% stake in Puma for €1.5 billion. Puma is a major supplier to Frasers’ Sports Direct chain, and the investment further expands Frasers’ portfolio of minority stakes in European fashion and retail brands. Private equity firm FSI is set to become the controlling shareholder of Italian luxury brand Missoni with a 73% stake, as the Missoni family exits its equity position. Katjes International will also acquire a 27% stake through its subsidiary Katjes Quiet Luxury. The transaction, expected to close in Q2 pending regulatory approval, positions FSI as the majority owner while giving Katjes the option to increase its stake in the future. Missoni CEO Livio Proli will remain in his role as the brand continues its growth strategy. Dallas-based private equity firm Trive Capital has made a strategic investment in women’s occasionwear brand Adrianna Papell. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in 1980 and headquartered in New York, Adrianna Papell designs cocktail, evening, and daywear styles and has sold more than 40 million dresses globally. The brand distributes through direct channels and retail partners across 27 countries. With Trive’s backing, the company plans to expand into new product categories, grow its direct-to-consumer and international presence, and pursue strategic acquisitions. The existing management team will continue to lead the business. Ashley Stewart has secured $15 million in new funding to support its next phase of growth and operational expansion. The plus-size fashion retailer plans to use the capital to strengthen its digital capabilities, enhance customer experience, and invest in strategic initiatives aimed at long-term brand development. The funding reinforces Ashley Stewart’s position in the inclusive fashion market as it continues to focus on omnichannel growth and deeper engagement with its core customer base. Outopia, a Chinese outdoor performance brand co-founded by a former Lululemon executive, has closed a Series B funding round led by Meridian Capital (Huaying Capital), with participation from Challenjers Venture, Ventech China, and Shunwei Capital. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in 2021 by Aaron Jackson, former director of raw material innovations and advanced concepts at Lululemon, and Alexis Hou, a former LVMH Asia-Pacific executive, Outopia specializes in technical merino wool apparel focused on trail running. The brand operates in China, New Zealand, and Australia. The company has built recognition around its performance fabrics and functional design, positioning itself within the professional trail running segment while expanding its offline retail footprint and overseas presence. Investors highlighted Outopia’s combination of technical innovation and strong brand identity as key drivers of its growth trajectory. Debenhams Group has increased its planned capital raise from £35 million to £40 million, aiming to strengthen liquidity and optimize its capital structure as it advances its restructuring and growth plans. The new shares were issued at 18 pence each, representing a 5% discount to the February 17 closing price of 19 pence. The company is also in discussions with lenders regarding amendments to its debt facilities. “The increase will provide an improved capital structure and greater financial flexibility to execute the restructuring and generate value,” said CEO Dan Finley. The raise involves senior leadership, including Finley and co-founder and executive chairman Mahmud Kamani. Non-executive director Iain McDonald resigned with immediate effect following nine years with the company. Aritzia has acquired the Fred Segal brand from Fred Segal Family LLC. Financial terms were not disclosed. As part of the deal, the Vancouver-based retailer has also leased 8100 Melrose Avenue in Los Angeles, the brand’s original flagship location. The move supports Aritzia’s long-term U.S. expansion strategy while marking an effort to revive the storied California lifestyle label. Founded in 1961, Fred Segal became synonymous with “California cool,” pioneering experiential retail and serving as a cultural hub for fashion, celebrities, and television. The brand helped shape Los Angeles’ style identity for decades. “Fred Segal has long been a cultural touchstone in Los Angeles, a place where creativity, community and style converge,” said Aritzia CEO Jennifer Wong. “We are honored to steward and evolve this iconic brand for a new generation with the elevated experience and ‘everyday luxury’ that define Aritzia.” Aritzia plans to restore the Melrose property, including its signature ivy-covered façade, and transform the space into a new experiential retail destination combining curated product and immersive lifestyle elements. The acquisition follows Aritzia’s previous investment in menswear brand Reigning Champ, signaling its continued appetite for strategic brand expansion as it grows its U.S. footprint. The Very Group has extended and renewed its main debt facilities, securing funding through 2029 and 2030 after Carlyle became its controlling shareholder last year. Its £1.77 billion securitization facility has been extended to February 2029, and its £150 million revolving credit facility now runs to February 2030. Ratings on the securitisation notes were confirmed or upgraded by Fitch and DBRS. The company also reduced its overall debt by £150 million with support from Carlyle. The interest rate on its senior secured notes has been lowered from 13.5% to 9.75%, and their maturity extended to August 2030. CFO Edward Fry said the deal strengthens the balance sheet and gives the business a stable base for future growth and investment. Frasers Group is set to acquire a majority shareholding in Maxi Sport SpA, the Italian activewear and sporting goods retailer. The founding Sala family will retain a minority stake and continue in leadership roles as the business enters its next phase of growth. Founded in Italy, Maxi Sport operates 18 stores nationwide, including six flagship locations, and offers a broad assortment across premium sports, extreme sports, and winter gear. Frasers said the partnership will allow Maxi Sport to maintain its top-tier retail format while unlocking future growth opportunities for Sports Direct stores in the region. “Maxi Sport represents the pinnacle of premium sports retail in Italy, and this partnership is the next phase of that journey,” said Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray. Mumbai-based fashion quick commerce startup ZILO has raised $15.3 million in a funding round led by Peak XV Partners, with participation from existing investors InfoEdge Ventures and Chiratae Ventures, alongside Alteria Capital, Stride Ventures, and a group of angel investors. Founded by former Flipkart and Myntra executives Padmakumar Pal and Bhavik Jhaveri, ZILO promises 60-minute fashion delivery with features like home trials and instant returns. The platform currently partners with more than 200 fashion brands and is building a vertically integrated operating model focused on speed, assortment, and control. “This round validates our belief that fashion and speed don’t have to be trade-offs,” said co-founder and CEO Padmakumar Pal. “We’re building a new category where curated fashion meets the immediacy customers now expect.” Gordon Brothers has acquired the global LK Bennett brand and related IP assets from the Joint Administrators of LK Bennett Fashion Limited. The London-based heritage fashion label, founded by Linda Bennett in the 1990s, is celebrated for its refined British aesthetic, from limited-edition ready-to-wear to luxury shoes, bags, and accessories. “LK Bennett is a beloved heritage brand with a reputation for impeccable craftsmanship and quality,” said Tobias Nanda, Head of Brands at Gordon Brothers. “We are proud to steward the brand into its next phase of growth and bring its modern luxury to new global audiences.” Gordon Brothers plans to revitalize LK Bennett through an asset-light model, similar to its successful transformation of the Laura Ashley brand, by growing licensing, expanding e-commerce, and strengthening wholesale relationships. The firm will invest in new marketing strategies and product development to reinforce the brand’s position in the modern luxury space. LVMH has increased its ownership of Loro Piana to 94% through a €1 billion call option transaction, further deepening its ties with the Italian luxury brand. The move underscores LVMH’s confidence in Loro Piana’s long-term potential and strategic importance, now valuing the brand at €11 billion. Maria Luisa and Pier Luigi Loro Piana will remain on the board, ensuring the brand’s heritage is preserved. Loro Piana has become the third-largest fashion and leather goods business within LVMH, following Louis Vuitton and Dior, with estimated annual revenues of €2.5 billion. Frédéric Arnault, son of LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault, was appointed CEO of Loro Piana in 2025, signaling the brand’s rising prominence. Since LVMH’s initial investment in 2013, the value of Loro Piana is believed to have quadrupled, driven by double-digit growth, increased investment in retail, and expanded product offerings in leather goods and homewares. China-based Anta Sports has acquired a 29.06% stake in Puma for €1.5 billion ($1.78 billion), becoming the German sportswear company’s largest shareholder. The deal, struck with Artémis, the Pinault family’s holding company, values Puma shares at €35 each and is expected to close by year-end, pending regulatory approval. The investment comes as Puma works to revive sales and momentum under CEO Arthur Hoeld, a former Adidas executive. Shares surged up to 20% on the news before settling around 9% higher. Anta said it has no current plans to acquire Puma outright. The move is part of Anta’s global expansion strategy and builds on its track record of acquiring Western sports brands, including the 2019 consortium-led acquisition of Amer Sports. Analysts say the deal could unlock synergies, with Puma’s strength in Europe and Latin America complementing Anta’s Asia-focused presence. Lands’ End and WHP Global have announced a strategic joint venture that will see WHP acquire a 50% controlling stake in the Lands’ End brand’s intellectual property for $300 million in cash. As part of the agreement, Lands’ End will contribute all brand-related IP and license agreements to the JV, while retaining full operational control of its DTC and B2B businesses. WHP Global will lead global licensing and brand expansion. The proceeds will be used to fully repay Lands’ End’s $234 million term loan and support broader corporate initiatives. The JV aims to unlock brand value through WHP’s global licensing platform. Watches of Switzerland Group has acquired an 88% stake in Deutsch & Deutsch, a family-owned luxury watch and jewelry retailer based in Texas, with an option to acquire the remaining shares. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition adds four Rolex-authorized showrooms in El Paso, Laredo, McAllen, and Victoria to the London-based company’s U.S. footprint. These locations will continue to operate under the Deutsch & Deutsch name, preserving the retailer’s brand as it nears its 100-year anniversary. Watches of Switzerland said the acquisition strengthens its U.S. showroom network, now including 25 Rolex-anchored locations. The acquired stores generated $67 million in revenue in 2023, with profitability in line with the group’s U.S. business. “We have admired Deutsch & Deutsch for many years and see this value-accretive acquisition as an excellent complement to our existing U.S. showroom network,” said Brian Duffy, CEO of Watches of Switzerland Group. “We look forward to combining Deutsch & Deutsch’s local expertise with our platform as we continue to grow in this key market.” Authentic Brands Group has acquired Guess?, taking the fashion retailer private in a deal valuing the brand at approximately $6 billion in global retail-equivalent sales. The transaction gives Authentic 51% ownership of Guess?’s intellectual property, with the remaining 49% held by existing shareholders including Maurice Marciano, Paul Marciano, Nicolai Marciano, and Carlos Alberini. The Guess? operating company will remain independent under current management, continuing to guide global strategy from its Swiss headquarters. The brand generated $3.14 billion in revenue over the past year and will now become Authentic’s second-largest label. “Guess? is one of the rare global brands that has built extraordinary awareness and continued to evolve while staying true to its DNA,” said Jamie Salter, Founder, Chairman, and CEO of Authentic.
