article_title: Italy Continues to Confront Luxury Fashion’s Supply Chain Problem
sub_title: Italian authorities are ramping up efforts to tackle labor abuses in the luxury industry, signaling a new phase of regulatory scrutiny.
article_content: Italian authorities are deepening their crackdown on labor abuses in the luxury fashion industry, signaling a new phase of regulatory scrutiny that directly challenges the heritage and craftsmanship-centric narratives that luxury brands rely on. Some of the latest developments include the closure of Italy’s consumer protection investigation into Dior , the early termination of judicial administration over a Valentino unit , and most recently, a broader investigation that saw authorities seek governance and supply-chain documents from nine luxury companies – from Chanel and Goyard to Bulgari, Moncler, and Brunello Cucinelli – in connection with their product packaging. Italian authorities have continued to broaden their scrutiny of labor practices in the luxury supply chain , with the latest phase extending beyond individual workshops and manufacturers to the oversight systems employed by some of the industry’s biggest brands. Most recently, police visited the offices of nine luxury companies – including Chanel, Goyard, Bulgari, Moncler, Brunello Cucinelli, Etro, Stefano Ricci, Jacob Cohën, and Owenscorp Italia – seeking documents relating to governance and supply-chain controls after investigators traced packaging materials bearing the brands’ labels to Chinese-owned subcontractors accused of exploiting workers . Notably, none of the companies has been accused of wrongdoing, and prosecutors have not sought court-appointed administration for any of them. Instead, authorities are examining the companies’ supply-chain oversight as part of the broader investigation into alleged labor exploitation involving subcontractors . The latest development builds on a series of high-profile enforcement actions. Earlier this year, police in Milan arrested a Chinese national and shuttered a clandestine workshop on the city’s outskirts that produced clothing for unnamed fashion brands. The site was found to employ 10 Chinese workers, six of whom were unregistered and five of whom were living in Italy without legal status. According to authorities, the workers endured extreme conditions, laboring up to 90 hours per week for as little as €4 an hour while sleeping in makeshift, unhygienic dormitories inside the workshop. The investigation was triggered by a worker’s complaint after his hand was allegedly broken by an employer when he attempted to recover €10,000 in unpaid wages. It followed closely from a separate case involving Valentino. In May 2025, an Italian court placed Valentino Bags Lab under judicial administration after finding that it had subcontracted production to Chinese-owned firms that exploited workers. The court, however, lifted the measure early in April 2026 after Valentino strengthened its governance safeguards, introduced a more rigorous supplier qualification process, and enhanced its systems for monitoring and controlling its supply chain. The matter mirrored earlier judicial administration orders involving units of Armani and Dior after Milan prosecutors uncovered exploitative subcontracting networks in the production of luxury leather goods. Separately, Italy’s Competition Authority (“ AGCM “) closed its consumer protection investigation into a Dior-owned company after the brand agreed to a package of voluntary commitments stemming from judicial findings that exposed sweatshop-like conditions in subcontracted workshops producing luxury handbags. The investigation centered on whether Dior’s public representations regarding ethics, craftsmanship, and its supply chain could mislead consumers in light of the labor conditions uncovered within portions of its manufacturing network. Without establishing any infringement of consumer protection law, the AGCM accepted Dior’s commitments and closed the matter. Under the settlement, Dior agreed to strengthen its supplier selection and auditing procedures, enhance oversight throughout its supply chain, and contribute €2 million over five years to initiatives aimed at identifying and supporting victims of labor exploitation. “Dior remains committed to upholding our values of transparency and respect throughout our supply chain,” the company said in a statement. “We continue to closely monitor, and where appropriate, strengthen, our internal procedures to maintain fair and equitable working conditions for everyone who contributes, with great commitment and skill, to creating the finest quality Dior products.” What began with investigations into individual workshops and judicial administration orders involving certain luxury companies has evolved into broader scrutiny of the governance structures, supplier qualification procedures, auditing practices, and supply-chain controls luxury brands use to oversee their manufacturing networks. For luxury brands, the legal focus is no longer confined to the conditions uncovered inside a factory – it extends to the systems designed to prevent those conditions from arising in the first place. These developments are not isolated. Over the past several years Italian magistrates have exposed widespread abuse in the fashion and luxury sectors, prompting legal and administrative reforms aimed at closing the gap between luxury’s crafted image and the exploitative practices that often sustain it. A 2024 proposal from Milan’s court urges fashion companies to adopt stricter oversight procedures to ensure labor law compliance among suppliers. Italy is home to a dense network of small manufacturers – estimated to produce more than half of the world’s luxury goods , according to Bain & Company. While these workshops play a critical role in the industry’s global dominance, they also represent a vulnerability: a fragmented supply chain that allows major brands to outsource production with minimal visibility, creating fertile ground for labor abuses to flourish. Regulators are asking not only what happened inside supplier facilities but also whether luxury brands had adequate systems in place to detect and prevent labor abuses. And they are not just focusing on labor violations themselves but also on the systems luxury companies use to prevent them. Supplier qualification procedures, auditing practices, governance structures, and ongoing oversight have become central features of Italy’s enforcement strategy, reflecting a broader expectation that brands exercise meaningful control over increasingly complex supply chains. With authorities continuing to raid workshops, place luxury companies under judicial administration, resolve consumer protection investigations, and seek governance records from some of the industry’s biggest names, a clear pattern has emerged. Italy’s enforcement efforts have expanded beyond uncovering labor abuses themselves to scrutinizing whether luxury companies have implemented meaningful governance and oversight systems to prevent them. As the industry grapples with its social responsibilities, Italy’s message is clear: luxury cannot come at the cost of the law. Share

article_title: Sustainability Funding and M&A Tracker
sub_title: Here is a running timeline of the most notable fashion and luxury-focused sustainability and ESG M&A and investments.
article_content: Sustainability is reshaping investment across fashion and retail, as brands, manufacturers, and investors direct capital toward technologies and business models aimed at reducing the industry’s environmental footprint and adapting to a growing body of climate- and sustainability-focused regulation . Investment is flowing into textile recycling and circularity, next-generation materials, lower-impact manufacturing, supply-chain traceability, resale and repair infrastructure, and technologies designed to help companies measure and manage their environmental impact, against a backdrop of mounting scrutiny over sustainability claims and greenwashing . Against that backdrop, this tracker follows notable funding rounds, mergers and acquisitions, strategic investments, and other transactions involving sustainability-focused companies and initiatives with a meaningful connection to fashion, beauty, retail, and consumer goods. The running timeline provides a view of where capital is flowing across the sector and how the technologies, materials, and business models underpinning the industry’s sustainability efforts are evolving. French recycling startup Syntetica has raised $30 million in Series A funding to scale its patented nylon recycling technology and build its first commercial demonstration facility in France. The round was led by Bpifrance’s Ecotechnologies 2 fund, with participation from lululemon, MAS Holdings, SWEN Capital Partners, EQT Ventures, and several strategic family offices. Syntetica’s technology can recycle both Nylon 6 and Nylon 6,6 from mixed post-consumer textile waste without requiring prior separation, addressing a major barrier to textile circularity. The funding will support industrial-scale deployment of the technology in partnership with Michelin’s Centre for Sustainable Materials. “For decades, mixed nylon waste has been considered too complex and too expensive to recycle at scale,” said co-founder and CEO Marco Bertone. “This funding allows us to move from breakthrough chemistry to industrial reality and accelerate the transition to more circular materials.” Berlin-based reverse.fashion has secured a seven-figure extension to its pre-seed funding round from High-Tech Gründerfonds (HTGF). Founded in 2024, the company develops AI-powered textile sorting technology that uses computer vision, machine learning, and Digital Product Passport integration to automate the classification of used garments for reuse, resale, repair, upcycling, or recycling. The funding will support the commercial rollout of its co.sort software and line.sort automated sorting system. According to the company, its technology can increase sorting productivity by 40% and boost recovered value by 20%, helping accelerate circularity across the fashion industry Fashion sustainability data platform Carbonfact has acquired Berlin-based Vaayu as brands face growing pressure to comply with product-level environmental disclosure regulations. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. The acquisition combines Carbonfact’s network of more than 200 fashion brands, including On, Ganni, and The North Face, with Vaayu’s expertise in retail climate data and product-level emissions tracking. The combined platform will serve more than 300 apparel and footwear brands globally. Founded in 2020 by former Zalando sustainability executive Namrata Sandhu, Vaayu developed one of fashion’s earliest product-level carbon accounting platforms and was backed by Atomico and CapitalT. Carbonfact is backed by Alven, Headline, and Y Combinator. The companies said the merger will help brands prepare for upcoming regulations including Digital Product Passports, France’s Eco-Score framework, and California’s SB253 climate disclosure rules. Carbonfact also said it is developing AI-powered “Environmental Intelligence” tools to help fashion companies manage emissions data and sustainability compliance workflows at scale. French textile upcycling startup Losanje has raised €6.7 million in funding to expand production capacity and accelerate the industrialization of its garment upcycling platform. The round included support from existing investors UI Investissement and Crédit Agricole, alongside new backers including Lita, Evolem, and Albo. Public institutions including ADEME, Bpifrance, and the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté Region also participated. Founded by Simon Peyronnaud and Mathieu Khouri, Losanje specializes in transforming unsold and used garments into new products for fashion brands through automated cutting and industrial upcycling processes. “This round marks a pivotal step in the emergence of an industrial upcycling sector,” said co-founder Simon Peyronnaud. The funding will support production expansion, new industrial equipment, R&D, and the relocation of operations to a larger 2,500-square-meter facility in Nevers as the company aims to position upcycling as a scalable pillar of the circular fashion economy. Fashion-tech company unspun has raised $32 million in an oversubscribed Series B funding round led by DCVC, with participation from Lowercarbon Capital, E12, Decathlon, and SOSV. The company plans to use the funding to expand deployment of its Vega™ 3D weaving technology across Europe and North America. Founded in the U.S., unspun develops automated weaving systems capable of producing garments directly from yarn within minutes, aiming to localize apparel manufacturing while reducing waste, inventory, and carbon emissions across fashion supply chains. The company partners with brands and manufacturers focused on decarbonization and supply chain efficiency through low-impact, on-demand production models. Bestseller has invested $3 million into the Regenerative Fund for Nature to support regenerative agriculture initiatives in South Africa’s Eastern Cape. The fund, launched by Conservation International and Kering, with Inditex joining in 2023, works with local communities to restore ecosystems and promote sustainable farming practices. Bestseller’s investment will support projects led by sheep farmers and shepherds focused on restoring grasslands, improving soil health, enhancing animal welfare, and reducing climate-related risks. The initiative aligns with Bestseller’s Fashion FWD sustainability strategy, which integrates biodiversity and ecosystem restoration into its supply chain and long-term raw material sourcing efforts. The Bezos Earth Fund has announced $34 million in new grants to accelerate the development of sustainable, next-generation materials for the fashion and textile industry. The funding supports research into innovative fibers designed to replicate the look and performance of traditional materials like cotton, silk, and rayon, while improving environmental impact through biodegradability, reduced land use, and lower emissions. “That’s not just good for the planet. That’s the future of fashion,” said Vice Chair Lauren Sánchez Bezos. Grant recipients include: Columbia University ($11.5M), developing bacteria-grown textile fibers from agricultural waste in partnership with the Fashion Institute of Technology; University of California, Berkeley ($10M), creating biodegradable fibers inspired by spider silk; Clemson University ($11M), engineering next-generation cotton using gene editing and synthetic biology; and The Cotton Foundation ($1.5M), restoring a global non-GMO cotton seedbank. The initiative underscores growing momentum behind bio-based and circular materials as the fashion industry looks to reduce its environmental footprint while maintaining performance and scalability. Reju has secured €135 million in funding from the Dutch government’s NIKI program to support the development of an industrial-scale textile-to-textile regeneration hub at Chemelot Industrial Park. The project will focus on recycling polyester-based textiles into new, high-quality materials, helping reduce reliance on virgin inputs and divert waste from landfill and incineration. The regenerated output, branded as Reju Polyester, is expected to deliver around 50% lower carbon emissions compared to traditional polyester. “This award is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and our team,” said CEO Patrik Frisk. The funding will support both construction and operations, positioning the Chemelot facility as a blueprint for scaling circular textile infrastructure across Europe. UK-based Epoch Biodesign has raised $12 million in funding, with participation from lululemon, Kompas VC, Happiness Capital, Extantia, and Leitmotif, bringing total funding to over $50 million. The company is focused on solving one of fashion’s toughest challenges: recycling nylon 6,6 at scale. Its proprietary enzyme-based process uses AI and synthetic biology to break down waste nylon into its original monomers, enabling the production of virgin-quality materials without fossil inputs. Unlike traditional methods, it can process complex materials like blended textiles and coated fabrics. The funding will support the move from pilot to large-scale demonstration, advancing commercial production and industry partnerships. Rubi has raised $7.5 million in funding co-led by AP Ventures and FH One Investments, with participation from investors including H&M Group, Talis Capital, and CMPC Ventures. The round follows strong commercial momentum, including over $60 million in offtake agreements with fashion brands and manufacturers. The company is developing a proprietary enzyme-based platform that converts CO₂ into essential materials, enabling the production of textiles and other inputs without relying on fossil resources. Its modular system is designed to support more flexible, lower-cost manufacturing across industries. “We’ve now demonstrated this technology scales effectively and meets or exceeds customer product standards,” said CEO Neeka Mashouf. The funding will support scaling to industrial production and expanding applications across textiles, consumer goods, and chemicals. India-based startup Canvaloop has raised $1.43 million in funding led by GVFL, with participation from Rockstud Capital. Founded in 2020, the company converts agricultural waste into spinnable textile materials, including hemp, flax, banana, nettle, and pine-based fibers compatible with existing manufacturing systems. The funding will be used to scale production capacity from 30 to 300 tonnes per month, expand the team, and advance R&D in regenerative cellulose materials. Swiss biomaterials company Seprify has raised €13.4 million (CHF12.25 million) in a Series A funding round to scale its cellulose-based materials platform. The round included investors Inter IKEA Group, Una Terra, Zürcher Kantonalbank (ZKB), Cambridge Enterprise Ventures, and Kickfund, alongside other circular-economy-focused backers. Seprify develops high-performance cellulose ingredients designed as sustainable alternatives to traditional materials. The funding will support commercial production, expand industrial partnerships, and accelerate the deployment of bio-based materials across multiple industries. Nonprofit organization Soles4Souls has acquired Erren Recondition, a Netherlands-based footwear and apparel reconditioning company. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Founded in Arnhem and operating for more than 130 years, Erren Recondition provides services including mold cleaning, repairs, finishing, labeling, and packaging. The company will continue operating in Europe under the name Erren Recondition, a Soles4Souls company. The acquisition expands Soles4Souls’ ability to help brands and retailers extend product life, reduce waste, and support circularity initiatives by refurbishing footwear and apparel for resale, reuse, or donation. Colorado-based outdoor apparel company Jack and Sage has acquired the assets, intellectual property, and inventory of sustainable apparel brand Kastlfel. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition expands Jack and Sage’s presence in premium logo wear across national parks, ski resorts, and outdoor destinations while adding a line of sustainable basics including tees, knitwear, and headwear. Kastlfel is known for using 100% sustainable materials such as organic cotton and recycled fibers. The deal also includes a partnership with Kastlfel’s parent company Ecocentric Brands to continue sustainability-focused screen printing operations in Denver. UK startup Shellworks has raised $15 million in Series A funding to scale production of Vivomer, its 100% compostable alternative to plastic used in beauty packaging.The round was led by Alter Equity, with participation from Nat Friedman, JamJar, and existing investors Founder Collective, LocalGlobe, and Third Sphere. Vivomer, a biopolymer created through microbial fermentation, can be used to produce rigid or flexible packaging and fully biodegrades within about a year. Beauty brands including Unilever’s Wild, Hair by Sam McKnight, Wildsmith, and Sonsie are already using the material. Advanced biotechnology company Ecovia Bio has closed a Series B funding round led by Pointe Angels to expand production capacity at its Livonia, Michigan facility. The capital will support a major scale-up of the company’s AzuraBase and AzuraGel product lines, gamma polyglutamic acid (γ-PGA) and specialty biopolymers used in cosmetics, personal care, agriculture, and hygiene applications. These biodegradable materials are designed to replace conventional petroleum-based superabsorbent polymers (SAPs), which contribute to long-term landfill waste and microplastic pollution. “This funding enables us to meet immediate customer demand while building the infrastructure required to serve the hygiene sector at industrial scale,” said CEO Kousay Said. Swiss traceability startup Haelixa has secured €2 million in a Pre-Series A funding round to accelerate global expansion and deepen partnerships with textile brands. The round was led by Verve Ventures and Zurich Kantonalbank, with participation from 212 NexT Fund. Haelixa’s proprietary technology uses DNA markers to tag and trace raw materials and products throughout the supply chain, offering brands proof of origin and production transparency. The company aims to scale internationally and position its solution as a critical tool for supply chain integrity amid rising regulatory and consumer pressure. The investment supports Haelixa’s long-term strategy to work closely with brands across fashion and textiles seeking robust, science-based traceability. Sparxell, a University of Cambridge spinout developing bioinspired, plastic-free colourants, has raised €4.2 million ($5 million) in pre-Series A funding to commercialize its cellulose-based pigment technology. The round was led by SWEN Capital Partners’ Blue Ocean 2 fund, with support from Alpha Star Capital and Cambridge Enterprise. Founded by Dr. Benjamin Droguet and Professor Silvia Vignolini, Sparxell creates vibrant colours using natural cellulose crystals, mimicking the iridescence seen in butterfly wings. Its patented structural colour platform enables the production of biodegradable pigments, inks, glitters, sequins, and films without toxic chemicals or plastics. “This funding takes us from proof of concept to production and commercial launches,” said CEO Droguet. Tonne-scale manufacturing is expected by the end of 2026. Lenzing Group has acquired a controlling majority stake in Swedish innovation company TreeToTextile AB, strengthening its position in sustainable, wood-based specialty fibers. The transaction, completed through the issuance of new shares, deepens Lenzing’s investment in a patent-protected, highly scalable cellulosic fiber technology. H&M Group, Inter IKEA Group, Stora Enso, and LSCS Invest will remain minority shareholders, continuing to support the platform with market, consumer, and long-term strategic expertise. TreeToTextile’s process is positioned as a major technological advance in fiber production, offering improved sustainability, cost efficiency, and broad applicability across textile and nonwoven markets. With majority ownership, Lenzing will accelerate the development of a demonstration plant and prepare for a large-scale industrial facility. “TreeToTextile is among the world’s most advanced next-generation fiber technologies,” said Georg Kasperkovitz, COO of Lenzing Group. “We are fully committed to the joint scale-up and commercialization.” Retail circularity platform SuperCircle has raised $24 million in Series A funding to expand its AI-driven infrastructure for managing and monetizing textile waste. The round was led by Foundry with participation from BBG Ventures, Renewal Fund, and Elemental Impact. Headquartered in New York, SuperCircle partners with over 75 retailers, including J.Crew, GUESS, Reformation, FIGS, and Parachute Home, to power consumer trade-in programs and reverse logistics. Its technology analyzes item-level data to route goods through over 50 reuse and recycling streams, helping brands reduce write-downs, comply with regulatory shifts, and unlock new revenue from excess inventory. “With SuperCircle, we’re turning end-of-life into a value-generating phase of the product lifecycle,” said CEO and co-founder Chloe Songer. The funding will fuel product development, logistics expansion, and broader enterprise adoption as the company targets 1 billion diverted textiles by 2030. The Repsol Foundation has acquired a 14% stake in Coleo Network, the recycling division of Spanish textile circularity leader Coleo. The investment supports Coleo’s expansion plans across Europe, including the development of new industrial-scale waste management and recovery plants, and aligns with Repsol Foundation’s strategy of backing triple-impact projects focused on social inclusion, environmental protection and sustainable growth. Founded by CEO David Puyuelo, Coleo operates at the forefront of Europe’s textile recycling push. With more than 7 million tonnes of textile waste generated annually in the region – much of it still ending up in landfills or incineration – the company aims to industrialise circular solutions and reduce waste dependency. “This investment reflects our commitment to the triple-impact economy and advancing sustainability in strategic sectors like textile recycling,” said Repsol chairman Antonio Brufau. Brussels-based Resortecs has raised €6 million in Series A funding to accelerate the rollout of its Smart Stitch and Smart Disassembly technology across Europe. The funding will support the completion of the company’s first continuous industrial disassembly line and the deployment of five lines in total over the next five years. Resortecs’ patented thermal disassembly system is designed to streamline textile-to-textile recycling by enabling garments to be taken apart at scale without manual intervention. The company plans to increase its processing capacity tenfold to 3,000 metric tonnes per year by 2027, helping brands and manufacturers meet circularity goals and divert waste from landfill. Dutch biotech startup Qorium has secured €22 million in Series A funding to scale its cell-grown leather production, marking a pivotal step from R&D to commercial manufacturing. The round was led by Invest-NL and LIOF, with continued support from Brightlands Venture Partners and Sofinnova Partners, and backed by the European Commission’s InvestEU guarantee scheme. Qorium creates real leather from a few animal cells – eliminating the need for livestock farming while dramatically reducing waste, water use, and emissions. The new capital will fund the installation of bioreactor systems at its Maastricht facility and accelerate its go-to-market strategy. With €30 million raised to date, Qorium is positioning itself as a global leader in sustainable materials innovation, targeting one of the most polluting industries in the world with a scalable, science-backed solution. “We’re creating real leather that outperforms the traditional version – without the environmental or ethical cost,” said CEO Michael Newton. Global holding company Inside Out LLC has acquired sustainable clothing brand The Simple Folk, marking a key step in its mission to reshape business through purpose-driven growth. Known for its minimalist, environmentally conscious designs, The Simple Folk will now operate under new CEO Luis Gamardo and gain access to Inside Out’s global infrastructure and sustainability expertise. The brand will collaborate with WRAD, Inside Out’s impact consulting studio, to align future expansion with the group’s ‘Towards a Thriving Future’ framework—focusing on environmental health, social responsibility, and long-term systemic change “Clothing is more than fabric, it’s a reflection of principle and care,” said Gamardo. “Inside Out gives us the platform to scale that belief globally, without compromise.” With the acquisition, Inside Out continues its commitment to backing companies that prioritize trust, wellbeing, and environmental stewardship alongside profit. Cambridge-based biomaterials startup PACT has raised £16 million in a Series A round led by Forbion and HV Capital to scale production of Oval , its patented collagen-based alternative to plastic-derived leathers like PVC. The funding will support the launch of a 20-meter pilot production line and drive commercial roll-to-roll manufacturing from PACT’s Cambridge HQ. Founded in 2020 by organic chemist Dr Yudí Ding and physicist-engineer Niels Ramay, PACT aims to replace synthetic leathers with Oval, a luxurious, durable, and designer-friendly material made from natural cosmetic-grade collagen infused with herbal oils and extracts. Compared to conventional faux leather, Oval uses less water and slashes CO₂ emissions while maintaining high aesthetic and tactile standards. The science is only the first step, the real challenge is scaling beautifully and sustainably,” said CEO Dr Yudí Ding. “With Oval, we’re delivering both innovation and impact.” London-based startup SAGES has secured £190,000 in funding from the British Design Fund to accelerate commercialization of its biodegradable, food-waste-derived dyes, an eco-friendly alternative to synthetic dyes, which contribute an estimated 20% of global wastewater. Founded by Emily Taylor and Alice Simpson, SAGES is pioneering water-soluble, non-toxic dyes sourced from waste streams like onion skins, coffee grounds, blueberries, and avocado. The startup’s patented formulations meet industry standards for UV and wash fastness and work with existing dyeing infrastructure. Recent collaborations include Patrick McDowell’s London Fashion Week collection, trials with Bananatex and Story Mfg, and surface projects with James Burleigh. The new capital will support pilot-scale production, product development, and partnerships across fashion, interiors, and industrial textiles. “We’re working to replace petroleum-based colourants with scalable, biodegradable alternatives that align with both industry needs and environmental urgency,” said co-founder Emily Taylor. Vienna-based refurbed, a leading marketplace for professionally refurbished electronics, sportswear, and ghomeoods, has raised £44 million in a funding round led by Alex Zubillaga and Orilla, with follow-on participation from existing investors including Evli Growth Partners, Bonsai, Almaz, C4 Ventures, and Speedinvest. Founded in 2017, refurbed promotes sustainable consumption by extending product lifecycles through refurbishment. The platform has processed 9 million devices, served 4 million customers across 12 European markets, and claims to have prevented 350,000 tons of CO₂ emissions and 1,136 tons of e-waste. The new capital will fuel growth in the UK, a key focus market for refurbed’s next phase of European expansion. “We’re rethinking consumption and helping people choose sustainability without compromising on quality,” said co-founder Peter Windischhofer. Indian materials science startup AltMat has announced new funding from a global investor group including H&M Group, Fashion for Good, Rainmatter by Zerodha, and Turbostart, as it scales its sustainable fiber innovation, Altag. Made entirely from agricultural residue like leftover food crop stems, Altag is positioned as a high-performance, low-impact alternative to conventional fibers. The fresh investment will support AltMat’s next phase of growth: expanding grassroots sourcing from Indian farmers, strengthening R&D, and accelerating international market entry. “Investing in AltMat is not just about backing material innovation, but about enabling a shift in the way our industry sources at scale,” said Laura Coppen, Investment Manager at H&M Group’s New Growth & Ventures. Finnish sustainable materials company Spinnova has acquired full ownership of Woodspin and Suzano Finland from joint venture partner Suzano S.A. The deal grants Spinnova exclusive rights to wood-based Spinnova fibre production, along with key assets including refining equipment, MFC technology, and 18 Suzano Finland employees who will now join the company. The joint venture will be dissolved as part of the agreement. London-based startup ZERØTEC has secured £642,000 in pre-seed funding to combat fashion’s staggering $300 billion annual fabric waste problem. The round was led by Bethnal Green Ventures, with backing from SFC Capital, SCE Freiraum Ventures, Cranfield University Seed Fund, and angel investor Benjamin Manwaring. Founded by former sustainability consultant Nicholas Betts, ZERØTEC uses AI-driven pattern optimisation to cut material waste at the design stage, offering up to 15% material savings for brands. The technology aims to eliminate waste before production begins, a sharp contrast to downstream recycling solutions. “We’re on a mission to solve one of fashion’s most critical problems with patented AI solutions that deliver real material benefits,” said Betts. “Our platform helps brands embrace sustainability, cut costs, and finally bring transparency to the true impact of our clothes.” With more than 250 brands already piloting its platform—including Fortune 500 apparel giants, ZERØTEC is gaining momentum as a category-defining solution in sustainable fashion tech. French startup EverDye has secured €15 million ($18 million) in fresh funding to scale its low-emission textile dyeing technology. The round was co-led by Crédit Mutuel Innovation and Daphni, as the fashion industry faces mounting pressure to reduce its environmental footprint. Founded in 2021 and based near Paris, EverDye claims its patented process uses lower temperatures, less water, and works with existing dyeing machinery, helping manufacturers cut both carbon emissions and operational costs. “Our solution not only promotes sustainability but also significantly reduces operational costs for manufacturers,” said Philippe Berlan, CEO of EverDye. “In an era where energy costs are a critical survival factor, EverDye’s innovation is a game-changer.” Textile recycling startup Refiberd has landed fresh investment and strategic support from PDS Ventures, extending its recent momentum following a major innovation award win in June. The Cupertino-based company, known for its plug-and-play AI technology that identifies garment material composition, will use the backing to expand integration into global sorting and recycling operations. Refiberd’s AI addresses a longstanding bottleneck in textile recycling, accurately sorting fabrics by fiber content, and aims to work within existing infrastructure rather than build standalone facilities. “The real unlock for us with PDS is that they can play both sides, moving conversations forward with customers, and also backing us financially,” said Sarika Bajaj, co-founder and CEO. “That’s the difference between surviving versus not, especially as market conditions get more strained.” French biotech company Carbios has confirmed €72 million in funding to begin construction of its first industrial textile recycling facility in Longlaville, Lorraine. The financing includes €42.5 million in support from ADEME and regional authorities, enabling the company to move forward with a project previously delayed. The plant will scale Carbios’ patented enzymatic depolymerization technology for PET, aiming to recycle the equivalent of 300 million synthetic T-shirts or two billion colored plastic bottles into virgin-quality material annually. “The recent regulatory boost and strong customer interest give us the confidence to move forward decisively,” said Managing Director Vincent Kamel. “This is a major step toward industrializing a circular economy for plastics and textiles.” YiLab, the materials science company co-founded by Stanford nanotech pioneer Yi Cui, has closed an oversubscribed pre-A funding round, bringing its total funding to over $10 million. The investment will accelerate the global rollout of its textile innovation platform LifeLabs Design, which creates sustainable, temperature-regulating fabrics for apparel and accessories. Built on a decade of Stanford research, LifeLabs fabrics reduce energy use by helping wearers stay cool or warm without relying on HVAC systems. The new funding will support the launch of a state-of-the-art R&D and manufacturing facility in Asia to speed prototyping and scale production. “This funding marks a pivotal step in our mission to transform textiles into powerful climate solutions,” said YiLab CEO and Co-Founder Sophia Ou. Materials science startup Everbloom has raised over $8 million in funding to advance its proprietary biodegradable fibers made from upcycled protein-rich waste. The round was led by Hoxton Ventures, with participation from SOSV, Tuesday Capital, Clocktower Ventures, and Brussels-based Endgame Capital. Everbloom’s next-gen textile technology addresses a critical sustainability gap in fashion by transforming waste into high-performance, planet-friendly materials. The funding will support the company’s next growth phase, including upcoming collaborations with premium fashion partners. “Everbloom is pioneering a category-defining platform for sustainable textiles,” said Hoxton Ventures’ Hussein Kanji. “Their breakthrough innovation has the potential to reshape how the fashion industry sources materials, and we’re excited to help them scale globally.” UK-based next-gen recycled leather fiber innovator Gen Phoenix has raised $15 million in a funding round led by Material Impact, with a significant follow-on investment from Tapestry, Inc., owner of Coach, Kate Spade, and Stuart Weitzman. Tapestry increased its equity stake to 9.9%, nearly quadrupling its 2023 position, and signed a three-year supply agreement as part of the deal. The new funding will support global expansion, increased production capacity at Gen Phoenix’s UK facility, and the commercialization of its fully circular leather solution. The move strengthens Tapestry’s future-ready supply chain while reinforcing its leadership in sustainable innovation. “This investment reflects our belief in the power of innovation to drive both purpose and profit. Gen Phoenix’s platform enables circularity at scale—delivering high-quality materials that meet the style, performance, and impact expectations of today’s consumer,” said Scott Roe, Tapestry Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer. Paris-based biotech Faircraft has acquired key assets from California startup VitroLabs in a strategic move to accelerate the industrialization of in vitro leather. The deal gives Faircraft access to VitroLabs’ high-end cultured leather demonstrations and a portfolio of 30 international patents covering innovations in tissue engineering, including multi-layered skin cultivation and scalable cell growth. Faircraft, which merges biotech and materials science to create sustainable alternatives for fashion and leather goods, now positions itself as a leader in the emerging lab-grown leather sector. “This marks a strategic turning point,” said CEO and Co-Founder Haïkel Balti. “Our goal is to make in vitro leather a mark of prestige for the world’s top fashion houses.” London-based biotech startup Solena Materials has raised $6.7 million in Seed funding to scale production of its AI-designed synthetic protein fibres—positioned as a sustainable, high-performance alternative to traditional textiles. The round was led by Sir David Harding, with continued backing from SynBioVen and Insempra, bringing Solena’s total funding to $10.8 million. Spun out of Imperial College London in 2022, Solena engineers fibres at the molecular level using AI and microbial fermentation to fine-tune properties like strength, flexibility, and texture. “We’re creating protein sequences that don’t exist in nature to meet modern performance and manufacturing needs,” said CEO and Co-Founder Dr. James MacDonald. The new capital will fund a facility expansion near Imperial and support new fashion industry partnerships. London-based Arda Biomaterials has raised $5.25 million in seed funding to scale production of its sustainable, leather-like materials made from spent barley sourced from beer and whisky makers. The round was led by Oyster Bay Venture Capital, with participation from Clean Growth Fund, Kadmos Capital, and Green Angel Ventures. The funding will support the buildout of a new facility five times larger than its current space, enabling Arda to scale its first product, New Grain, a plastic- and animal-free textile for fashion and automotive use. Based in London’s Bermondsey Beer Mile, Arda has already partnered with BEEN London on a snakeskin-style handbag made with locally sourced grain waste. “We’re connecting brewers and distillers with the fashion and automotive worlds,” said cofounder and CEO Brett Cotten. “That’s where real scale and impact happen.” German startup eeden has raised €18 million in a Series A round to accelerate its chemical textile recycling technology. The round was led by Forbion’s BioEconomy Fund, with backing from Henkel Ventures, NRW.Venture, and returning investors TechVision Fonds, High-Tech Gründerfonds, and D11Z Ventures. Based in Münster, eeden has developed a proprietary chemical process that upcycles cotton-polyester blends by recovering cellulose and breaking down polyester into reusable building blocks. These can be converted into high-quality fibers like lyocell, viscose, and polyester—providing a circular alternative to conventional textiles. The funding will support construction of eeden’s demonstration plant in Münster, scale industrial processing, and advance commercial partnerships across the textile industry. “eeden has developed a pioneering solution that can make large-scale textile recycling not only technologically feasible but also commercially viable,” said Forbion’s Alex Hoffmann. London-based climatetech startup 51toCarbonZero has raised £3 million in a new funding round led by Fuel Ventures, with support from angel investors. The investment will fuel the company’s expansion into Europe and the U.S., and advance its AI-powered platform designed to help corporations manage and reduce their carbon emissions. 51toCarbonZero, whose clients include ETRO, Wolf, Sonobi, and KNESKO Skin, offers a solution that meets rising demands for emissions transparency and regulatory compliance. “We’ve built a platform that empowers businesses to make real progress toward net zero,” said the team. Fuel Ventures, a returning investor, reaffirmed its confidence in the company’s mission and rapid growth. Trove has acquired Reverse.supply, a Berlin-based resale marketplace, as part of its strategy to expand internationally and strengthen its technology offering for brands implementing circular solutions. The deal, the terms of which have not been disclosed, follows Trove’s acquisition of Recurate in August 2024 and positions the resale technology company to better serve growing demand across Europe, the UK, and North America. “The timing of this transaction is pivotal, as brands and retailers in Europe are facing new legislation and actively seeking profitable, future-proof revenue streams,” said Janis Künkler, Co-Founder of Reverse.supply. “By bringing Trove’s proven technology to Europe, we’re positioned to help brands navigate these changes and build successful resale programmes.” Simplifyber, a startup developing bio-based alternatives to traditional textiles, has raised $12 million (€10.5 million) in a funding round led by Suzano Ventures. The company’s proprietary material, Fybron, is both biodegradable and designed for 3D injection molding—eliminating the need for spinning, weaving, cutting, or sewing in the production of soft goods. The funding will support scientific development, mechanical engineering, and expanded production, as well as new facilities and strategic partnerships. Simplifyber recently partnered with Danish fashion brand Ganni to produce a shoe upper made entirely from its material, marking an early step toward commercial adoption. Paris-based Fairly Made, a scale-up driving sustainability in fashion, has raised €15 million in funding to accelerate its evolution into a pure technology player. The round was led by BNP Paribas Solar Impulse Venture Fund, along with GET Fund, ETF Partners, and Frenchfounders. “This funding allows us to scale our SaaS platform, expand our expert team, and support global growth,” said co-founder Laure Betsch. Fairly Made’s 360° platform enables fashion brands to track supply chains, assess environmental impact, and increase consumer transparency. The company currently supports clients including LVMH, Versace, A.P.C., and Paul Smith. Sheep Inc has raised £5 million ($6.48 million) in a Series A funding round led by Inside Out LLC.
