article_title: AI Goes Shopping: Inside the New Era of Agentic Commerce
sub_title: Looking ahead, big companies in the tech, retail, and financial services segments are touting the next phase of “agentic commerce.”
article_content: Buying and selling online via traditional e-commerce is old news. The market is entering the age of A-commerce, where artificial intelligence (“ AI ”) is increasingly able to shop for consumers. At the end of September, OpenAI launched its “ Buy it in ChatGPT ” trial in the United States, using AI agents built to interact with consumers to do more of people’s browsing and shopping. The technology is known as “ agentic commerce.” ChatGPT already helps millions of people find what to buy. Now it can help them buy it too,” ChatGPT announced late last month. “We’re introducing Instant Checkout in ChatGPT with  Etsy and Shopify, and open-sourcing the Agentic Commerce Protocol that powers it, built with  Stripe, so more merchants and developers can integrate agentic checkout.” In short: American shoppers can now ask for shopping suggestions from U.S. Etsy sellers within a ChatGPT chat – then buy a product immediately, without having to navigate away to look at individual shop pages. Looking ahead, big companies in the tech, retail, and financial services segments are touting the next phase of “autonomous agentic commerce.” Experts predict that the emerging shopping model in which AI agents act on behalf of customers could come into effect to a meaningful extent within the next few years. For most people using AI to help them shop, the AI agent is still mostly just searching and recommending products. It still has to shift the customer to the retailer’s website to complete the checkout. For instance, AI can do most steps to order a pizza – though sometimes slower than consumers doing it themselves – apart from paying at the end. That is where individuals still step in: Buyers still need to sign in and/or enter personal and delivery details and then pay. And that is part of what agentic AI aims to eliminate. With the “Buy it in ChatGPT” trial now underway in the U.S., the customer never leaves the chat, where the checkout is completed. Shopify has said more than 1 million of its merchants will soon be able to check out within ChatGPT, too. Retail titan Walmart has similar plans. In May 2025, Google launched “ AI mode shopping .” Some features, like using a full body photo of yourself to virtually “try-on” clothes, are still only available for U.S. shoppers, with limited brands. At the time, Google said its next step will be a new “agentic checkout […] in coming months” for products sold in the US. It would give shoppers the option of tracking a product until its price drops to within a set budget – then automatically prompting them to buy it, using Google Pay. That checkout option is yet to launch . Credit card giants Visa and Mastercard are working on ways to make it easier for AI agents to shop for consumers.  And American Express is actively building and partnering with other tech and financial companies to enable agentic commerce. Both the current and coming forms of agentic commerce have the potential to spread fast worldwide, because they run largely on the same global digital infrastructure powering today’s e-commerce: identity, payments, data and compliance. In a report this month, McKinsey revealed that Agentic AI “promises to radically remake the entire shopping experience,” stating that by 2030, the U.S. B2C retail market, alone, “could see up to $1 trillion in orchestrated revenue from agentic commerce, with global projections reaching as high as $3 trillion to $5 trillion.” “We’re entering an era where AI agents won’t just assist – they’ll decide,” McKinsey asserts. This presents both benefits and risks for today’s commerce ecosystem, per McKinsey. “The transition from static e-commerce to a more dynamic agentic commerce system unlocks transformative potential, redefining customer experiences and operational agility.” In particular, AI agents can create personalized offers that align with a customer’s budget and aesthetic. Subscription-based businesses may see particular gains as agents handle recurring orders automatically, while dynamic pricing systems can fine-tune prices in real time based on demand and competition. Beyond customer engagement, these systems also optimize back-end functions like logistics and inventory, turning AI agents into a force for holistic operational and value transformation. But these potential gains are not with risks. There are straightforward risks, such as overspending, as agentic commerce removes many steps of the shopping journey found in e-commerce or physical commerce, leading to fewer abandoned carts and potentially higher spending. There is also the risk of fraud, which means that banks will need to figure out how to spot fraud, process refunds, and manage consent when it is not a person pressing “buy,” but an algorithm doing it on their behalf. Then there are more novel risks, including those that center on customer trust and relationships, since consumers would need to trust AI systems with their private data and preferences , and ensure they are not misused. Against that background, regulators will need to consider agentic commerce in their competition, privacy, data, and consumer protection rules. Even for small business, the way products are made and services are discoverable online will have to change in the age of agentic AI. Instead of having websites built for customers and search engines, businesses will need to build AI accessible online stores. Those will not necessarily look like the websites of today; they will be more akin to data-soaked digital catalogues, filled with everything an AI agent needs to place orders: product specifications, price, stock, ratings, reviews, through to delivery options. Years of bigger brands buying attention and dominating search results might start to matter a bit less if upstarts are able to build good AI accessible online stores. It could be a quiet but massive shift in how trade works. However, each business’s visibility will depend on how AI systems read and rank sellers. If a business’s data is not formatted for AI, it may disappear from view. That could give larger players an edge and once again make it harder for smaller businesses to compete. Ultimately, this new wave of commerce raises questions for companies and consumers, alike. How willing are consumers to delegate our shopping to AI agents? And are businesses – from brands, retailers and marketplaces to logistics and commerce services providers and payments players – willing and able to adapt to the new paradigm in order to successfully navigate the challenges of trust, risk, and innovation? Vibhu Arya is a PhD Student in the UTS Business School at the University of Technology Sydney. (Additions courtesy of TFL.) Share

article_title: Fashion & Retail Funding and M&A Tracker
sub_title: Here is a running timeline of the most notable fashion, retail, activewear, and luxury-focused M&A and investments.
article_content: M&A and investments continue to dominate the fashion and luxury industries, with a rise in deal volume driven by ongoing consolidation, digital acceleration, and rising pressure on margins. From strategic acquisitions to tech-driven funding rounds, the landscape is increasingly shaped by players aiming to future-proof their operations and expand global reach. Big-name deals over the past several years have brought Tiffany & Co. under the umbrella of LVMH (after the two companies managed to put their rival lawsuits to bed and come to agreeable terms under which French conglomerate could acquire the famed New York-based jewelry stalwart); ridded Richemont of loss-making Yoox Net-a-Porter ; and saw Farfetch acquired in a rescue deal by Korea e-commerce giant Coupang. These moves come amid growing urgency around consolidation, with giants like LVMH, Kering, and Richemont sharpening their portfolios and tech stacks. Sources close to recent transactions suggest more tie-ups are in the pipeline, especially as mid-sized brands and service providers look for scale or exit opportunities in a high-cost, high-competition environment. “Whether it’s automation, data-driven pricing, or owning more of the value chain, the current deal flow shows the industry’s pivot toward resilience and agility,” says one sector analyst. As fashion grapples with evolving consumer behavior, cost pressures, and digital disruption, the M&A and funding landscape is set to remain active well into 2025 and beyond. With the foregoing in mind, here is a tracker of the most recent fashion and retail-focused M&A and investments … Samsonite Group agreed to acquire an 85% stake in Béis, the travel and luggage brand founded by actress and entrepreneur Shay Mitchell, for $178.5 million, valuing the company at $210 million. The acquisition expands Samsonite’s portfolio of travel brands, which includes TUMI, High Sierra and Gregory. Founded in 2018, Béis generated approximately $210 million in net sales in 2025. Mitchell will remain chief creative officer and retain a 15% stake, while majority shareholder Beach House Group will sell its 70% interest. Samsonite plans to leverage its global distribution, sourcing and logistics capabilities to accelerate Béis’ growth while maintaining the brand as a standalone business. “Joining the Samsonite Group gives us the chance to dream even bigger,” said Shay Mitchell, founder and chief creative officer of Béis. Frasers Group acquired luxury department store Harvey Nichols out of administration for an undisclosed amount, ending 35 years of ownership by Hong Kong billionaire Dickson Poon. The transaction includes six UK stores, the company’s e-commerce operations, inventory and international franchise agreements, with more than 1,000 employees transferring to Frasers. The acquisition adds another prominent retail brand to Frasers’ portfolio, which includes House of Fraser, Evans Cycles and Sofa.com. Frasers plans to restructure Harvey Nichols to restore the loss-making retailer to sustainable growth, potentially reviewing its store footprint, organizational structure and cost base. “The turnaround will require tough choices, and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term,” said Michael Murray, CEO of Frasers Group. Scalpers has acquired a stake in Spanish youth fashion brand Yuxus to support its domestic and international expansion. Financial terms and the size of the stake were not disclosed. Yuxus, founded eight years ago by brothers Guillermo and Álvaro Ferre, operates 14 stores and employs nearly 100 people. The founders will remain involved in management, while Yuxus gains access to Scalpers’ resources to strengthen existing markets and enter new countries. The investment advances Scalpers’ strategy of building a portfolio of high-growth fashion brands, which already includes Victoria, Mim Shoes and Deeply. The transaction data comes from Dealroom.co, citing Forbes España as the original source. MondeVita has acquired a majority stake in Underscore District, the Milan-based brand accelerator behind Magliano, GR10K and WOK Store. Financial terms were not disclosed. The transaction follows MondeVita’s acquisition of menswear manufacturer Raffaele Caruso and adds brand development, merchandising, retail and e-commerce capabilities to its growing Italian luxury platform. Underscore District generated more than €7 million in sales in 2025 across a wholesale network of over 150 retailers. CEO Edoardo Di Luzio will remain in place and take on a broader strategic role within MondeVita, while the group plans to support Magliano’s international expansion and pursue additional luxury acquisitions. “We are building a platform where creativity and established craftsmanship reinforce one another, and Underscore District is central to that design,” said Fabio Brambilla, chairman of MondeVita. Canada Goose Holdings has agreed to sell Baffin Limited, its Canadian performance footwear brand, to L.P. Royer, a Canadian manufacturer of work and military footwear. Financial terms were not disclosed, and the transaction is expected to close in August, subject to customary closing conditions. Canada Goose acquired Baffin in 2018 as its first move into footwear, using the acquisition to build expertise and infrastructure as it expanded beyond outerwear. Founded in 1979, Baffin specializes in technical footwear designed for demanding environments and has established a strong reputation for performance, durability and Canadian craftsmanship. Under Royer’s ownership, the brand will join another long-established Canadian footwear manufacturer with expertise across industrial, mining, construction and military applications. “This transaction is about focus. We’ve made meaningful progress evolving Canada Goose into a year-round lifestyle brand, and this gives us the opportunity to continue that momentum by simplifying our operating model, focusing resources on our highest-priority opportunities and drive long-term profitable growth,” said Dani Reiss, Chairman & CEO of Canada Goose. WME Group has sold the New York Fashion Week, NYFW and NYFW: The Shows trademarks and intellectual property to Signet Fashion, including associated websites and social media assets. Financial terms were not disclosed. Signet plans to expand the NYFW platform through live programming, digital content, media production, brand partnerships and year-round audience engagement. “We welcome Signet’s investment and look forward to seeing how its efforts help create new opportunities for designers and contribute to the continued success of New York Fashion Week,” said Steven Kolb, President and CEO of the CFDA. LVMH has sold Patou to Nirvana Investments LLC-FZ, the holding company of Dubai-based entrepreneur and Designer Parfums founder Dilesh Mehta. Financial terms were not disclosed. LVMH originally acquired a majority stake in Patou from Mehta in 2018, with Mehta retaining a 30% interest, and subsequently relaunched the historic French maison as a fashion label after roughly three decades of dormancy in fashion. The transaction returns control of Patou to Mehta following a period of leadership changes, including the departures of CEO Sophie Brocart in 2024 and artistic director Guillaume Henry in February 2026. “We now look forward to building on that foundation and continuing Patou’s growth with the same long-term vision, respect for its heritage and ambition for the future,” said Dilesh Mehta. Crown Brands Group has acquired Italian luxury lingerie brand Cosabella from CALIDA GROUP, marking its second acquisition in seven months following the purchase of Hanky Panky. The deal expands Crown’s premium intimates portfolio and supports its strategy of acquiring heritage consumer brands with global growth potential. “Cosabella is everything we look for in a brand: true Italian craftsmanship, a devoted customer, and a name that means something in every major market,” said Raymond Dayan, CEO of Crown Brands Group. UK retailer Frasers Group has increased its stake in Hugo Boss to approximately 30.28%, crossing the threshold under German takeover rules that requires a mandatory takeover offer. Frasers acquired an additional 2.55 million shares, up from its previous 26.06% holding, reinforcing its position as Hugo Boss’ largest shareholder. The move follows Frasers’ €2 billion (€38 per share) takeover proposal in June, which Hugo Boss urged shareholders to reject as “financially inadequate.” Frasers said its offer remains open through July 27. A Hugo Boss spokesperson said the increased shareholding “does not have any implications for the voluntary takeover offer or the offer process.” UK womenswear brand Never Fully Dressed has sold a minority stake to Refined Capital Partners in its first external investment since founder Lucy Aylen launched the business in 2009. Financial terms were not disclosed. The investment will support the brand’s future growth while allowing its existing leadership team to remain in place. Refined Capital Partners’ portfolio includes The Fold, Frugi, Disturbia, Celtic & Co, and Turtle Doves. In a statement, Never Fully Dressed described the deal as “an exciting milestone,” adding: “We’re still the same female-founded brand, led by the same leadership team, designing every print in-house with the same passion, creativity and attention to detail.” The company said the partnership will enable further investment in the business and strengthen its commitment to its people, sustainability efforts, and long-term expansion. French running retailer i-Run has acquired Belgian running and trail specialist Trakks, expanding its presence in the Benelux region. Founded by Christophe Thomas, Trakks operates six stores and an e-commerce platform, generating €7.1 million in revenue and €0.7 million in net profit in 2025. The acquisition will see Trakks rebranded as “Trakks by i-Run”, with integration into i-Run’s systems scheduled for October. Trakks’ founders will remain with the business for at least two years to support the transition and drive i-Run’s regional growth. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Chanel has acquired Charvet, the historic French luxury shirtmaker, strengthening a relationship that dates back to founder Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel, who famously purchased Charvet shirts for Arthur “Boy” Capel. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Founded in 1838, Charvet is renowned for its bespoke shirts and craftsmanship, employing around 100 people across its Paris flagship and French production workshop. The acquisition follows creative director Matthieu Blazy’s collaboration with Charvet on Chanel’s Spring 2026 collection, which featured oversized cotton shirts that became standout pieces of the season. Chanel said the deal will preserve Charvet’s heritage and craftsmanship while ensuring its long-term future. “We decided to get married. We thought it made sense for the future of Charvet to be secured by Chanel,” said Bruno Pavlovsky, President of Fashion and President of Chanel SAS. “It’s part of our legend and storytelling.” Damiani Group has completed its acquisition of Baume & Mercier from Richemont, adding the 200-year-old Swiss watchmaker to its portfolio of luxury jewelry and watch brands. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The acquisition strengthens Damiani’s position in hard luxury and expands its watchmaking business. The group plans to increase Baume & Mercier’s global visibility by leveraging its international distribution network and selectively opening mono-brand boutiques, while Richemont will continue providing operational support during the integration period. “The Damiani Group is uniquely positioned to realise Baume & Mercier’s full potential… We are confident to have found in Damiani Group the right home for Baume & Mercier to thrive in years to come,” said Nicolas Bos, Chief Executive Officer of Richemont. HSG has completed its acquisition of Italian luxury footwear brand Golden Goose, becoming the company’s majority shareholder in a deal that values the business at nearly $2.5 billion. Temasek is also joining the transaction as a strategic minority investor through True Light Capital. As part of the ownership transition, former Gucci chief Marco Bizzarri has been appointed non-executive chairman, effective immediately, while CEO Silvio Campara will remain in his role. The deal formalizes a transaction first announced last year and comes as Golden Goose continues to post growth, with first-quarter revenue rising 10% year over year to €173.2 million. Italian luxury group OTB has acquired the remaining stake in Viktor&Rolf, taking full ownership of the Dutch fashion house founded by Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren. Financial terms were not disclosed. OTB first acquired a majority stake in Viktor&Rolf in 2008 and increased its ownership to 70% in 2019. The transaction completes OTB’s long-term investment in the brand, while the founders will remain in place as creative directors under an agreement extended last year. Known for its avant-garde haute couture, ready-to-wear, bridalwear, eyewear, and fragrance business with L’Oréal Luxe, Viktor&Rolf becomes a wholly owned part of OTB’s luxury portfolio, which includes Diesel, Jil Sander, Maison Margiela, Marni, and Amiri. UK online flash-sales retailer BrandAlley has been rescued through a pre-pack administration deal, with the business, brand, website, and ongoing operations acquired by BrandAlley International Ltd. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The restructuring follows financial difficulties at BrandAlley and is expected to preserve the majority of operations. Of the company’s 163 employees, 15 have been made redundant, with approximately 60 additional roles expected to be affected following completion of the ownership transfer. According to the company, customer operations will continue uninterrupted, with existing orders, returns, and refunds being honored as normal. The deal secures the future of one of the UK’s best-known online off-price fashion and lifestyle retailers while allowing the business to continue trading under new ownership. Digital fashion startup Meta Fashion has raised approximately $400,000 in a pre-seed funding round led by Lumikai, with participation from investors including Big Bets, Anton Gauffin, Akshat Rathee, and Pratham Mittal. Founded in 2022 by Arjun Goel, the company develops digital fashion assets for platforms including Roblox, Fortnite, and ZEPETO, while also building its own Roblox-based game, GlamGirls. Meta Fashion said it has sold more than 2.5 million virtual fashion items on Roblox, generating nearly $300,000 in GMV. The company plans to use the funding to expand across UGC gaming platforms, scale its virtual fashion business, and grow its GlamGirls IP. Gordon Brothers has acquired British handbag and accessories brand Radley and its related intellectual property as part of its growing portfolio of heritage fashion and lifestyle brands. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in London’s Camden Market in 1998, Radley built a strong presence in accessible luxury through its handbags and accessories business. Gordon Brothers said it plans to pursue an asset-light, licensing-led growth strategy focused on expanding the brand across the U.S., U.K., Australia, and Asia while broadening categories beyond handbags into watches, jewelry, eyewear, and beauty gifting. “We are thrilled to add another British icon to our global portfolio of brands,” said Tobias Nanda, Head of Brands at Gordon Brothers. The acquisition further expands Gordon Brothers’ fashion brand portfolio, which already includes Nicole Miller, LK Bennett, Rachel Zoe, and Laura Ashley. Authentic Brands Group has signed a definitive agreement to acquire heritage denim label Lee from Kontoor Brands, further expanding its portfolio of global fashion and lifestyle brands. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded more than a century ago, Lee generates approximately $1.5 billion in annual retail sales across 73 countries. Following the acquisition, Authentic plans to transition the business to its licensing-driven operating model, leveraging its global network of partners to expand the brand across apparel, experiences, and lifestyle categories. “What makes Lee so compelling is its legacy,” said Authentic founder and executive chairman Jamie Salter. “It’s one of the most important names in denim.” The transaction is expected to close in the second half of 2026, subject to regulatory approval and customary closing conditions. Marquee Brands has signed a deal to acquire a majority interest in Roberto Cavalli through a strategic partnership with DAMAC Group, which will remain a significant shareholder. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition adds Roberto Cavalli to Marquee Brands’ growing portfolio of lifestyle and fashion brands and expands its presence in luxury fashion, bringing total portfolio-wide retail sales to approximately $5 billion. “Roberto Cavalli stands as one of luxury’s defining Italian houses,” said Marquee Brands CEO Heath Golden. As part of the transaction, Milan-based The Level Group will oversee product development, retail, e-commerce, and wholesale operations for the brand across Europe and the U.S. Artemis, the holding company controlled by the Pinault family and owner of Kering, has agreed to sell its majority stake in Giambattista Valli back to founder Giambattista Valli as part of a broader effort to streamline investments and reduce debt. Financial terms were not disclosed. The move follows Artemis’ recent sale of a 29% stake in Puma to Anta Sports Products for €1.5 billion earlier this year. “This agreement now allows me to regain full control of my brand,” Valli said in a statement. The transaction comes amid continued pressure across the luxury sector as weaker global demand weighs on independent high-end fashion brands. The s.Oliver Group has acquired the Baldessarini brand rights from New Baldessarini GmbH, a subsidiary of R.Brand Group, as part of its strategy to strengthen its premium menswear offering. Financial terms were not disclosed. Baldessarini will operate as an independent label within s.Oliver’s growing House of Brands portfolio alongside Lala Berlin, while helping expand the group’s position in contemporary tailoring and premium casualwear. “Baldessarini is a strong brand with great potential,” said s.Oliver Group co-CEO Johannes Rellecke. “With it, we are closing the gap between classic business wear and modern casual menswear.” The relaunch of Baldessarini under the s.Oliver umbrella is planned for early 2027. Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein is set to acquire direct-to-consumer apparel brand Everlane in a deal reportedly valued at around $100 million, according to reports. The transaction follows months of financial pressure at Everlane, which reportedly carried roughly $90 million in liabilities, including a $25 million loan from Gordon Brothers and a $65 million revolving credit facility. Majority shareholder L Catterton and CEO Alfred Chang had reportedly explored outside investment options before Shein opted for a full acquisition. Puck reported that holders of Everlane common stock are not expected to receive proceeds from the transaction, though details regarding preferred shareholders were not disclosed. The acquisition would give Shein ownership of a well-known U.S. contemporary fashion label as the company continues expanding beyond its fast-fashion roots and deepening its global retail footprint. LVMH has agreed to sell Marc Jacobs to a joint venture formed by WHP Global and G-III Apparel Group, with the buyers raising up to $850 million to finance the acquisition. Under the deal, WHP Global and G-III will each contribute up to $425 million, with WHP overseeing licensing operations and G-III managing the brand globally. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. The sale marks the end of LVMH’s nearly 30-year ownership of Marc Jacobs, which it acquired in 1997. Founder Marc Jacobs will remain creative director following the transaction. The acquisition expands WHP Global’s premium fashion portfolio, which already includes Vera Wang, rag & bone, and G-STAR, while reflecting broader consolidation trends in the accessible luxury market. Castore has secured a £90 million credit facility from HSBC UK, BNP Paribas, and Lloyds to support retail expansion in the UK and accelerate growth across key international markets in the Middle East and Asia. The Manchester-based sportswear brand plans to use the financing to expand its store footprint and strengthen its position as a global premium performance apparel company. Castore is targeting more than £300 million in sales over the next financial year. “This new funding provides us with the flexibility and ability to accelerate our retail rollout,” said co-founder Tom Beahon. Founded in 2015, Castore has attracted backing from investors including Andy Murray and INEOS, and recently acquired heritage fashion brand Belstaff for approximately £102 million. Kering has announced it will acquire a minority stake in Shanghai-based Icicle Fashion Group as part of a strategic partnership with its parent company ICCF. Founded in 1997, Icicle is a fast-growing Chinese luxury brand with more than 200 stores globally, including a presence in Paris, and has been expanding into Western markets. The investment reflects Kering’s continued focus on strengthening its position in China while supporting the international growth of local luxury brands. Financial terms were not disclosed. Kering and L’Oréal have finalized their strategic beauty partnership, confirming L’Oréal’s €4 billion acquisition of Kering Beauté, including the House of Creed, along with long-term fragrance and beauty licenses for Kering’s luxury Houses. The agreement also includes plans to explore new opportunities in wellness and longevity through a joint venture, signaling a broader expansion beyond traditional beauty categories. “Our strategic alliance with L’Oréal marks a decisive step forward for Kering,” said CEO Luca de Meo. For L’Oréal, the deal strengthens its leadership in luxury beauty, building on its longstanding success with brands like Yves Saint Laurent Beauté while unlocking new growth opportunities across Kering’s portfolio. Perfect Moment has secured $12 million in growth financing to strengthen its balance sheet and support its path to sustainable profitability. The package includes a $10 million revolving credit facility from Krane Capital and X3 Higher Moment Fund, alongside a $2 million equity investment from Krane Capital, priced at a 75% premium to the company’s recent share price. The funding follows the brand’s first profitable quarter and will be used to enhance liquidity, invest in product innovation, and expand into new categories and markets. A key focus is China, where Krane Capital’s local expertise is expected to support distribution and market entry within the premium segment. “This financing enhances our financial flexibility and supports continued expansion across our key initiatives,” said Executive Chairman Max Gottschalk. American Exchange Group has agreed to acquire the assets of Allbirds in a $39 million deal, marking a dramatic reset for the once high-flying sustainable footwear brand. The transaction, expected to close in Q2 2026 pending shareholder approval, will include the winding down of Allbirds’ public company structure. The deal follows a sharp decline in performance, with the company reporting a 23.3% drop in quarterly revenue and continued losses, alongside the closure of its remaining U.S. stores. Originally launched in 2016 and once valued at over $4 billion, Allbirds rose quickly on the strength of its minimalist wool sneakers before struggling with rapid expansion and strategic missteps. “This next chapter… sets up the brand to thrive in the years ahead,” said CEO Joe Vernachio. For American Exchange Group, the acquisition adds to a growing portfolio of fashion and lifestyle brands, signaling continued consolidation in the footwear and apparel sector. Sandbridge Capital, a private equity firm focused on consumer and luxury investments, has taken a 5% stake in  Jacquemus. The transaction involves the sale of the founder’s personal shares, rather than new capital being injected into the business. It follows L’Oréal’s earlier investment of around 10%, supporting Jacquemus’ planned expansion into beauty, including a cosmetics line set to launch in 2027. Despite new investors, founder Simon Porte Jacquemus retains majority ownership. London-based fashion distributor and brand incubator Tomorrow Ltd. has been acquired by Progetto 11, the parent company of Italian e-commerce platform The Level Group. Financial terms were not disclosed, though existing investor Three Hills Capital Partners is reported to have taken a loss on its stake. Founded as a showroom business, Tomorrow evolved into a brand incubator with stakes in labels including Coperni and Martine Rose, supporting production, development, and distribution. However, the company has faced mounting challenges in recent years, including declining revenues, liquidity pressures, and tensions with partner brands. “The focus of the board has been to guarantee protection and continuity for the business,” said founder Stefano Martinetto. The acquisition is expected to stabilise operations and integrate Tomorrow into The Level Group’s broader e-commerce and logistics platform, though the future of its brand partnerships remains uncertain. French rainwear brand Flotte has raised €2.5 million in funding from Time4, a new investment fund launched by Daphni and Les Déterminés. The funding will support the brand’s growth and expansion as it continues to scale its sustainable outerwear offering. Founded as a specialist rainwear label, Flotte focuses on functional, eco-conscious apparel designed for urban lifestyles. Online retailer Quince has raised $500 million in a Series E funding round led by ICONIQ Capital, with participation from Basis Set Ventures and Wellington Management. The round values the company at $10.1 billion. The San Francisco–based platform sells apparel, jewelry, and home goods through a manufacturer-to-consumer model that removes traditional retail intermediaries. Its AI-driven platform forecasts demand and produces goods in smaller batches to reduce excess inventory. Quince reported more than $1 billion in revenue in 2025 and plans to use the new funding to support global expansion of its technology-enabled retail model. Frasers Group has acquired a 5.8% stake in German sportswear company Puma, according to regulatory filings. The position was largely built through derivatives tied to roughly 8.5 million shares. If exercised, the stake would make Frasers Puma’s second-largest shareholder behind the Pinault family. The move follows Anta Sports’ agreement earlier this year to purchase a 29% stake in Puma for €1.5 billion. Puma is a major supplier to Frasers’ Sports Direct chain, and the investment further expands Frasers’ portfolio of minority stakes in European fashion and retail brands. Private equity firm FSI is set to become the controlling shareholder of Italian luxury brand Missoni with a 73% stake, as the Missoni family exits its equity position. Katjes International will also acquire a 27% stake through its subsidiary Katjes Quiet Luxury. The transaction, expected to close in Q2 pending regulatory approval, positions FSI as the majority owner while giving Katjes the option to increase its stake in the future. Missoni CEO Livio Proli will remain in his role as the brand continues its growth strategy. Dallas-based private equity firm Trive Capital has made a strategic investment in women’s occasionwear brand Adrianna Papell. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in 1980 and headquartered in New York, Adrianna Papell designs cocktail, evening, and daywear styles and has sold more than 40 million dresses globally. The brand distributes through direct channels and retail partners across 27 countries. With Trive’s backing, the company plans to expand into new product categories, grow its direct-to-consumer and international presence, and pursue strategic acquisitions. The existing management team will continue to lead the business. Ashley Stewart has secured $15 million in new funding to support its next phase of growth and operational expansion. The plus-size fashion retailer plans to use the capital to strengthen its digital capabilities, enhance customer experience, and invest in strategic initiatives aimed at long-term brand development. The funding reinforces Ashley Stewart’s position in the inclusive fashion market as it continues to focus on omnichannel growth and deeper engagement with its core customer base. Outopia, a Chinese outdoor performance brand co-founded by a former Lululemon executive, has closed a Series B funding round led by Meridian Capital (Huaying Capital), with participation from Challenjers Venture, Ventech China, and Shunwei Capital. Financial terms were not disclosed. Founded in 2021 by Aaron Jackson, former director of raw material innovations and advanced concepts at Lululemon, and Alexis Hou, a former LVMH Asia-Pacific executive, Outopia specializes in technical merino wool apparel focused on trail running. The brand operates in China, New Zealand, and Australia. The company has built recognition around its performance fabrics and functional design, positioning itself within the professional trail running segment while expanding its offline retail footprint and overseas presence. Investors highlighted Outopia’s combination of technical innovation and strong brand identity as key drivers of its growth trajectory. Debenhams Group has increased its planned capital raise from £35 million to £40 million, aiming to strengthen liquidity and optimize its capital structure as it advances its restructuring and growth plans. The new shares were issued at 18 pence each, representing a 5% discount to the February 17 closing price of 19 pence. The company is also in discussions with lenders regarding amendments to its debt facilities. “The increase will provide an improved capital structure and greater financial flexibility to execute the restructuring and generate value,” said CEO Dan Finley. The raise involves senior leadership, including Finley and co-founder and executive chairman Mahmud Kamani. Non-executive director Iain McDonald resigned with immediate effect following nine years with the company. Aritzia has acquired the Fred Segal brand from Fred Segal Family LLC. Financial terms were not disclosed. As part of the deal, the Vancouver-based retailer has also leased 8100 Melrose Avenue in Los Angeles, the brand’s original flagship location. The move supports Aritzia’s long-term U.S. expansion strategy while marking an effort to revive the storied California lifestyle label. Founded in 1961, Fred Segal became synonymous with “California cool,” pioneering experiential retail and serving as a cultural hub for fashion, celebrities, and television. The brand helped shape Los Angeles’ style identity for decades. “Fred Segal has long been a cultural touchstone in Los Angeles, a place where creativity, community and style converge,” said Aritzia CEO Jennifer Wong. “We are honored to steward and evolve this iconic brand for a new generation with the elevated experience and ‘everyday luxury’ that define Aritzia.” Aritzia plans to restore the Melrose property, including its signature ivy-covered façade, and transform the space into a new experiential retail destination combining curated product and immersive lifestyle elements. The acquisition follows Aritzia’s previous investment in menswear brand Reigning Champ, signaling its continued appetite for strategic brand expansion as it grows its U.S. footprint. The Very Group has extended and renewed its main debt facilities, securing funding through 2029 and 2030 after Carlyle became its controlling shareholder last year. Its £1.77 billion securitization facility has been extended to February 2029, and its £150 million revolving credit facility now runs to February 2030. Ratings on the securitisation notes were confirmed or upgraded by Fitch and DBRS. The company also reduced its overall debt by £150 million with support from Carlyle. The interest rate on its senior secured notes has been lowered from 13.5% to 9.75%, and their maturity extended to August 2030. CFO Edward Fry said the deal strengthens the balance sheet and gives the business a stable base for future growth and investment. Frasers Group is set to acquire a majority shareholding in Maxi Sport SpA, the Italian activewear and sporting goods retailer. The founding Sala family will retain a minority stake and continue in leadership roles as the business enters its next phase of growth. Founded in Italy, Maxi Sport operates 18 stores nationwide, including six flagship locations, and offers a broad assortment across premium sports, extreme sports, and winter gear. Frasers said the partnership will allow Maxi Sport to maintain its top-tier retail format while unlocking future growth opportunities for Sports Direct stores in the region. “Maxi Sport represents the pinnacle of premium sports retail in Italy, and this partnership is the next phase of that journey,” said Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray. Mumbai-based fashion quick commerce startup ZILO has raised $15.3 million in a funding round led by Peak XV Partners, with participation from existing investors InfoEdge Ventures and Chiratae Ventures, alongside Alteria Capital, Stride Ventures, and a group of angel investors. Founded by former Flipkart and Myntra executives Padmakumar Pal and Bhavik Jhaveri, ZILO promises 60-minute fashion delivery with features like home trials and instant returns. The platform currently partners with more than 200 fashion brands and is building a vertically integrated operating model focused on speed, assortment, and control. “This round validates our belief that fashion and speed don’t have to be trade-offs,” said co-founder and CEO Padmakumar Pal. “We’re building a new category where curated fashion meets the immediacy customers now expect.” Gordon Brothers has acquired the global LK Bennett brand and related IP assets from the Joint Administrators of LK Bennett Fashion Limited. The London-based heritage fashion label, founded by Linda Bennett in the 1990s, is celebrated for its refined British aesthetic, from limited-edition ready-to-wear to luxury shoes, bags, and accessories. “LK Bennett is a beloved heritage brand with a reputation for impeccable craftsmanship and quality,” said Tobias Nanda, Head of Brands at Gordon Brothers. “We are proud to steward the brand into its next phase of growth and bring its modern luxury to new global audiences.” Gordon Brothers plans to revitalize LK Bennett through an asset-light model, similar to its successful transformation of the Laura Ashley brand, by growing licensing, expanding e-commerce, and strengthening wholesale relationships. The firm will invest in new marketing strategies and product development to reinforce the brand’s position in the modern luxury space. LVMH has increased its ownership of Loro Piana to 94% through a €1 billion call option transaction, further deepening its ties with the Italian luxury brand. The move underscores LVMH’s confidence in Loro Piana’s long-term potential and strategic importance, now valuing the brand at €11 billion. Maria Luisa and Pier Luigi Loro Piana will remain on the board, ensuring the brand’s heritage is preserved. Loro Piana has become the third-largest fashion and leather goods business within LVMH, following Louis Vuitton and Dior, with estimated annual revenues of €2.5 billion. Frédéric Arnault, son of LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault, was appointed CEO of Loro Piana in 2025, signaling the brand’s rising prominence. Since LVMH’s initial investment in 2013, the value of Loro Piana is believed to have quadrupled, driven by double-digit growth, increased investment in retail, and expanded product offerings in leather goods and homewares. China-based Anta Sports has acquired a 29.06% stake in Puma for €1.5 billion ($1.78 billion), becoming the German sportswear company’s largest shareholder. The deal, struck with Artémis, the Pinault family’s holding company, values Puma shares at €35 each and is expected to close by year-end, pending regulatory approval. The investment comes as Puma works to revive sales and momentum under CEO Arthur Hoeld, a former Adidas executive. Shares surged up to 20% on the news before settling around 9% higher. Anta said it has no current plans to acquire Puma outright. The move is part of Anta’s global expansion strategy and builds on its track record of acquiring Western sports brands, including the 2019 consortium-led acquisition of Amer Sports. Analysts say the deal could unlock synergies, with Puma’s strength in Europe and Latin America complementing Anta’s Asia-focused presence. Lands’ End and WHP Global have announced a strategic joint venture that will see WHP acquire a 50% controlling stake in the Lands’ End brand’s intellectual property for $300 million in cash. As part of the agreement, Lands’ End will contribute all brand-related IP and license agreements to the JV, while retaining full operational control of its DTC and B2B businesses. WHP Global will lead global licensing and brand expansion. The proceeds will be used to fully repay Lands’ End’s $234 million term loan and support broader corporate initiatives. The JV aims to unlock brand value through WHP’s global licensing platform. Watches of Switzerland Group has acquired an 88% stake in Deutsch & Deutsch, a family-owned luxury watch and jewelry retailer based in Texas, with an option to acquire the remaining shares. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition adds four Rolex-authorized showrooms in El Paso, Laredo, McAllen, and Victoria to the London-based company’s U.S. footprint. These locations will continue to operate under the Deutsch & Deutsch name, preserving the retailer’s brand as it nears its 100-year anniversary. Watches of Switzerland said the acquisition strengthens its U.S. showroom network, now including 25 Rolex-anchored locations. The acquired stores generated $67 million in revenue in 2023, with profitability in line with the group’s U.S. business. “We have admired Deutsch & Deutsch for many years and see this value-accretive acquisition as an excellent complement to our existing U.S. showroom network,” said Brian Duffy, CEO of Watches of Switzerland Group. “We look forward to combining Deutsch & Deutsch’s local expertise with our platform as we continue to grow in this key market.” Authentic Brands Group has acquired Guess?, taking the fashion retailer private in a deal valuing the brand at approximately $6 billion in global retail-equivalent sales. The transaction gives Authentic 51% ownership of Guess?’s intellectual property, with the remaining 49% held by existing shareholders including Maurice Marciano, Paul Marciano, Nicolai Marciano, and Carlos Alberini. The Guess? operating company will remain independent under current management, continuing to guide global strategy from its Swiss headquarters. The brand generated $3.14 billion in revenue over the past year and will now become Authentic’s second-largest label. “Guess? is one of the rare global brands that has built extraordinary awareness and continued to evolve while staying true to its DNA,” said Jamie Salter, Founder, Chairman, and CEO of Authentic. As a private company, Guess? will have more flexibility and access to resources to support growth. Richemont has signed an agreement to sell Baume & Mercier to Italy’s Damiani Group, marking a major move in the luxury watch sector. Applied Real Intelligence (A.R.I.), a U.S.-based growth investment firm, has made a strategic investment in October’s Very Own (OVO), the lifestyle brand founded by Aubrey “Drake” Graham, Oliver El-Khatib, and Noah “40” Shebib. Marubeni Corporation has acquired UK-based Jacobson Group, owner of heritage sneaker brand Gola, as part of its strategy to build a scalable lifestyle brand platform anchored by R.G. Barry Corporation (RGB). The acquisition marks RGB’s first roll-up deal since Marubeni acquired it in 2024. Jacobson’s portfolio, led by Gola, a British brand founded in 1905 with strong roots in sport and fashion, is distributed in over 30 countries. Marubeni’s Consumer Platform U.S. is focused on building next-generation consumer businesses under the company’s GC2027 strategy. Italian luxury apparel company Zanieri has completed its reverse merger with Everlert, Inc. (OTC: EVLI), gaining control of the public entity and integrating its operations under the Everlert corporate structure. Temasek will join as a minority investor, alongside existing backer Permira, which will retain a strategic minority position. The deal supports Golden Goose’s international growth while preserving its Italian craftsmanship roots. CEO Silvio Campara will continue to lead the company, with Marco Bizzarri (ex-Gucci CEO) becoming Non-Executive Chairman. MadaLuxe Group has acquired a majority stake in IPPOLITA, the New York-based fine jewelry house known for its sculptural designs, artisanal craftsmanship, and global following. The deal adds to MadaLuxe’s expanding portfolio of luxury fashion and lifestyle brands across categories including apparel, accessories, home, and spirits. The acquisition aligns with MadaLuxe’s strategy to invest in heritage-driven brands with enduring cultural relevance. IPPOLITA founder Ippolita Rostagno will continue as Chief Creative Officer, leading design across the brand’s signature 18k gold and sterling silver collections. “Joining MadaLuxe opens an exciting new chapter that protects our heritage while embracing new growth,” said Rostagno. The brand, which debuted at Bergdorf Goodman, has become a defining name in accessible fine jewelry and is sold through top luxury retailers worldwide. Newly launched luxury group Hulcan, founded by MILE co-founders Joe Wilkinson and Mario Maher, has acquired iconic fashion retailer MATCHES and its in-house label RAEY. The deal marks a major move in redefining the future of luxury commerce, with the two brands set to relaunch in 2026 under Hulcan’s innovative, omnichannel model. The acquisition includes the full IP portfolio of MATCHES, positioning Hulcan to revive and evolve the storied retailer with a sharper focus on profitability, digital transformation, and cultural relevance. Backed by investors including Frasers Group, Francesco Ragazzi, PagsGroup, LVMH Luxury Ventures Advisors, and the Hermès Family, Hulcan aims to integrate commerce, culture, media, and fashion in a single ecosystem. “We’re committed to preserving MATCHES’ legacy while transforming it for a new era of luxury,” said Maher. “This acquisition is foundational to building a connected, modern group that serves both brands and the next generation of luxury consumers.” Global asset advisory firm Gordon Brothers has acquired a majority interest in the intellectual property of the Rachel Zoe brand, aiming to accelerate its growth through expanded licensing, new product categories, and broader distribution. The investment solidifies Rachel Zoe’s evolution from celebrity stylist to influential lifestyle entrepreneur with a multi-channel media and consumer brand. Best known for her Bravo show The Rachel Zoe Project and editorial platform The Zoe Report, Zoe has built a business spanning apparel, home, fragrance, eyewear, and children’s products. She continues to lead the brand as Founder, Chief Creative Officer, and board member. “Rachel is a global fashion authority with a brand that resonates across style, media, and lifestyle,” said Tobias Nanda, Head of Brands at Gordon Brothers. “We’re excited to grow her legacy through strategic licensing and innovation.” Republic Brands Group (RBG) has acquired heritage fashion labels Joie, Equipment, and Current/Elliott for $36 million, forming a new division dubbed The Lux Group. The move marks a strategic expansion for RBG as it builds a portfolio of culturally resonant, commercially proven brands. RBG plans to pivot the labels from a retail-heavy model to a focus on DTC and wholesale, while expanding into new categories such as handbags, footwear, and accessories through licensing. Skims, the shapewear and apparel brand co-founded by Kim Kardashian and Jens Grede, has raised $225 million in a new funding round led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, with participation from BDT & MSD Partners. The raise values the brand at $5 billion as it accelerates plans for product expansion, international growth, and a deeper push into physical retail. Global investment firm Carlyle has officially taken control of The Very Group, marking the end of the Barclay family’s more than 20-year ownership of the UK-based online retail giant. Abu Dhabi-based IMI, another major lender, remains a key stakeholder in the business. Homecourt, the luxury home care brand founded by Courteney Cox in 2022, has raised $8 million in Series A funding to scale its team, expand retail partnerships, and prepare for international growth. International expansion is on the horizon, with London eyed as a potential launch point. “This brand works because I won’t settle for 99 percent,” Cox said. “It has to be perfect.” French e-commerce player Showroomprivé is divesting its 51% stake in fashion platform The Bradery, selling it back to founders Timothée Linyer and Edouard Caraco for €43.6 million. Showroomprivé will receive an initial €17 million payment, with additional proceeds tied to performance-based milestones. The transaction is expected to close by year-end, pending regulatory approvals. Chalhoub Group has made a strategic minority investment in the menswear brand Willy Chavarria, joining existing investor FAE Fashion Ventures. The deal, reportedly under $5M, supports the label’s continued global expansion and infrastructure development. Chavarria, known for his culturally conscious, identity-driven collections, will benefit from Chalhoub’s deep operational expertise and regional retail presence across the Middle East. Founder and CEO Laure Hériard Dubreuil will retain a minority stake and continue to lead operations. Colorado-based outdoor brand Halfdays has raised $10 million in a Series A round led by Kellwood Company, with participation from Dick’s Sporting Goods Ventures, model Taylor Hill, and others. Known for redefining women’s skiwear with a stylish, functional edge, Halfdays was co-founded by Ariana Ferwerda, Karelle Golda, and Olympian Kiley McKinnon. The brand, which has gained traction over the past five years, is now shifting from survival mode to growth mode. “It’s the difference between surviving and scaling,” said Ferwerda, reflecting on the milestone moment. Fueled by strong seasonal performance and high sell-through rates, the funding will support expansion of Halfdays’ winter and ski lines, entry into year-round performance wear, accelerated wholesale partnerships with retailers like Revolve and Shopbop, and investments in brick-and-mortar retail. DK Company has acquired a majority stake in German fashion brand IVY OAK, expanding its presence in the premium fashion segment and strengthening its position in the German market. As part of the deal, IVY OAK’s headquarters will relocate to Copenhagen under DK Company’s structure, while the brand’s creative studio will remain in Berlin. “With IVY OAK, we see a perfect match between a strong, design-driven brand and DK Company’s expertise in international marketing and distribution,” said Jens Obel, CEO and co-owner of DK Company. “This acquisition supports our strategy of investing in the premium segment, while staying true to the creative and sustainable DNA of the brand.” German fashion label Closed has officially found new owners following insolvency proceedings. The Böck family, known for their role in Marc O’Polo, and fashion executive Dieter Holzer have acquired the company in a strategic move to revive the premium denim and lifestyle brand. Closed’s headquarters will remain in Hamburg, ensuring continuity for its operations and team. The acquisition secures the future of the brand, which has long been known for its high-quality craftsmanship and contemporary European aesthetic. Details of the restructuring plan or future strategy have not yet been disclosed, but the new owners are expected to focus on stabilizing operations, strengthening wholesale and retail presence, and rebuilding brand equity across core markets. Artistic Milliners has acquired a majority stake in Cone Denim from Elevate Textiles, forming a new multinational entity that will operate under the iconic Cone Denim name. VF CEO Bracken Darrell added, “This transaction supports our strategy to strengthen our balance sheet and focus on core growth opportunities.” Kering and Mayhoola “ jointly announce that they have agreed to amend their shareholders’ agreement (initially concluded at the time of Kering’s acquisition of a 30% stake in Valentino in 2023) and more specifically the framework of the evolution of Valentino’s shareholding. Gemfields Group has sold luxury jeweller Fabergé Ltd to SMG Capital for $50 million as part of its strategy to streamline operations. Known for its ornate, jewelled eggs, Fabergé was acquired by Gemfields in 2012 to complement its coloured gemstone business and leverage the brand in jewellery marketing. The sale follows a strategic review launched late last year. Outzidr, the digital-first fashion brand catering to Gen Z women in India, has raised Rs 27 crore (approximately $3.1 million) in a pre-Series A round led by RTP Global, with participation from existing backer Stellaris Venture Partners. Founded in 2024, Outzidr launched in February 2025 with a trend-led western wear lineup targeting women aged 18–28. Known for its fast-paced test-and-scale model, the brand has already released over 8,000 styles and served 100,000+ customers in just five months, with retention rates 1.5x above industry benchmarks. The new capital will support Outzidr’s expansion into offline retail, with its first exclusive store set to open by March 2026, alongside investments in design, tech, and operations. “We’re building a brand that listens, learns, and reacts in real time,” said co-founder and CEO Nirmal Jain. Adanola, the U.K.-based cult womenswear brand redefining the active lifestyle wardrobe, has received a significant minority investment from Los Angeles-based private equity firm STORY3 Capital Partners. The deal, which values Adanola at approximately $530 million, marks a major milestone in the brand’s global growth journey. “This investment supports our vision to scale Adanola as a global leader in the active lifestyle category while building sustainable, profitable growth across key markets,” said CEO Niran Chana. Fashion-tech start-up ANNY has raised Rs. 10 crore ($1.15 million) in a Pre-Series A funding round led by early-stage investor Atomic Capital. Founded in 2003 by Japjot Singh (CEO), Aveen Kaur (COO), and Rahul Tanwar (CTO), ANNY operates a vertically integrated, inventory-light business model focused on trend-led fashion in the accessible luxury market in India. “With the support of Atomic Capital, we are not only scaling faster but also scaling smarter,” said Singh, adding that the investment will help fuel ANNY’s goal of becoming a Rs. 100 crore+ ARR brand by next year. Apoorv Gautam, Founder of Atomic Capital, praised ANNY’s operational excellence, strong consumer affinity, and capital-efficient growth trajectory. LVMH Luxury Ventures – the private equity arm of French luxury giant LVMH – has acquired a minority stake in Molli, the historic French knitwear house relaunched in 2014.
